text:
Mauro Mina (pictured, coming in at 45-2-2) hands a young (11-1-0 coming in) Bob Foster his 2nd career loss on November 7, 1963 in Lima, Peru. 

Foster had lost his first fight in 1962 to heavyweight Doug Jones.

 Mina had Foster down for an 8-count in the 9th round of this fight.

Mauro Mina, born in Chincha, in 1933, is considered by most to be the greatest Peruvian boxer of the 20th century. He'd almost certainly be an alphabet titlist today.

Mina would go 10-2-1 in his first thirteen fights and then go on an unbeaten streak from April of 1959 to September of 1964. 

Mina would score wins over Gregorio Peralta, Henry Hank, Eddie Cotton and Foster during that streak. In 1960 Mina was proclaimed the South American Light Heavyweight Champion, a title he held until he vacated it in 1966.

Mina's three career defeats were to: Peralta, a heavyweight, to Luis Agnicio in only his 7th pro fight -  Agnicio is considered the greatest Brazilian light heavyweight of all time - and to Dogomar Martinez in his 13th fight. Martinez lost only three fights and had represented Uruguay in the 1948 Olympic Games.

Mina, 52-3-3 with 25 KO's, was one of the very best fighters to never fight for a world title. 

He retired, due to a detached retina, in 1965.
----------------------------------------------------------
From Boxing Insider on Mauro Mina, it's a long read but worth your attention regarding an excellent boxer so few remember or know about. You definitely won't read about him in the boxing groups that I've come and gone from over the past several years:

Angelo Dundee: Mauro Mina Would Have Been A Champion in Any Era!
By: Ken Hissner

The film “Imagining Mina” is a bittersweet, yet inspiring story about the great 1960’s Peruvian boxer Mauro Mina. This multilayered film follows Mina’s unlikely journey – from the cotton fields of rural Peru to Madison Square Garden. Set in the context of mid-twentieth century Latin America, the film also analyses the world in which Mina lived and the obstacles he faced. He was Afro-Peruvian and faced racism prior boxing from 1955 to 1965 until his death in 1993 at the age of 59.
Within the movie it tells how Mina was dedicated himself to boxing. He would talk to whoever called on him, rich or poor. He created his own world. For a President of Peru the former General Ricardo Perez Godoy to intervene in the career of an athlete because he was Mauro Mina and the economic impact was obvious. He awarded Mina with a Gold watch.
Mina’s mother left when he was an infant. His father doted on him but passed away when Mina was 7. He lived with his grandparents and the step-grandmother Susana beat him almost daily. After his grandfather passed when Mina was 12 he moved back in with his mother. A local friend of his mother’s had him work in the slaughter house. He became very strong at a young age. He went to school at 11 and quit at 14 to work full time. He went to Lima to box on an amateur show and decided to stay with an aunt and never see his mother again.
How Mina got started boxing was when he would pass by a group of boy’s each day who set up a gym on the outside. It took three times of asking him before he tried boxing. By the time he was 15 he was known as a knockout artist. When he was 17 he was asked to move to Lima to continue his amateur career. He moved to there and lived with his aunt never seeing his mother again. At 20 he joined the military thinking his boxing career was going nowhere.
He experienced racism as a descendent of Africans, the manipulation of the media and the curious politics of the boxing business. “Imagining Mina” weaves candid, first-hand accounts, newly recorded digital images; and rare archival images; to recreate the captivating story of common man who became a national icon and international sensation. Alfredo Bejar directed and promoted this film. This writer purchased this DVD telling the story to get the full depth from start to finish.
As an amateur Mina won the Latin American Games middleweight title in 1952. He won his first 6 professional bouts and by nearing the 2 year mark boxing his promoter Max Aguirre who as a promoter received criticism and an equal amount of praise. Mina had only fought 10 rounds so when it was decided to see what he was made of his promoter took him to Sao Paulo, Brazil to fight Luis Ignacio, 22-2-1. Mina scored a first round knockdown but lost a close decision.
Mauro Mina, Jr., today said of his father “he’d say I’m going to bring the sun for the light. And the sun would come out, by coincidence. He won people over.” He was getting robbed by those managing him only giving him $50-100 while fighting 10 round bouts. He may not have been making much money but he was fighting often.
“Life told me something” he would say. He would settle with an old ally who offers to help named Oscar Teran who would become his manager. He knew things and knew Aguirre who said “I’ll manage you, not Max. When I tell you something you do it.” His brother Alejandro said “he was a beautiful person. He was like a father to Mauro and involved with the government industry where he had contacts and was well off. He began to manage Mina without pay. Will Mauro be a South American champion which meant a lot to the Peruvian people? He defeated Antonio Diaz, 49-10-17, twice. He had a rematch with Ignacio in July of 1958 which ended in a draw in Lima.
Mina was matched with the South American champion Dogomar Martinez, 46-2-5, in Montevideo, Uruguay. “I trained just like before otherwise I wouldn’t make such a long trip. The problem was Martinez was also well prepared. He got a new trainer in Otto Salas. Mina looked quicker, He used his right hand more. “Before I had to tie his left hand so he’d work only with his right,” said Salas. Mina starts out countering and by the fourth round Martinez becomes more aggressive. Martinez was awarded the fight 6-4-5. Martinez said “that’s a future champion.”
On Mina’s return to Lima the journalists started their criticism saying “he doesn’t have the making of a champion.” Shortly after fighting Martinez he was driving with a friend who had an accident leaving Mina with a scar on his right cheek. Joe de Leon from Panama was considered to become his trainer. “For a long time, 30 years, until he got the opportunity to train the star of Peru, Mauro Mina,” said Joe de Leon, Jr.
A foreign executive came to Lima to run the phone company for IT & T. He became Mina’s sponsor and gave him a job. He agreed to have de Leon train him but said Mina was getting a new trainer with each fight and needed to stick with just one. “I’ll train him only if he wants me to train him. First I’ll train him, he’ll fight and if my work is satisfactory we’ll talk about compensation,” said de Leon. He was a class act, a real gentleman.
With all the pieces in place Mina returned to the ring after 6 months to face one of Argentina’s top prospects named Rodolfo Diaz, 4-0-1, defeating him in back to back fights. Mina was knocked down in the first fight which would be the only time during his career he was knocked down. “Rodolfo Diaz by the way was one hell of a fighter. He was a sturdy guy with a great chin. He had a big heart and was determined to hang in there. He wasn’t discouraged easy and made good fights. For Mina to lick this guy twice was quite an achievement,” said Hank Kaplan, Boxing Historian.
“De Leon taught him how to fight inside, up close and how to bob and weave. He was no longer a stiff boxer. He knew how to dodge and connect inside”, said Dr. Pamarino. (Former sparring partner) “My father said Mauro was too nice. He was too nice of a guy. To inspire to be a champion he had to make him nastier and turn him into an aggressive guy without being mean. He simply took on the attributes of a champion,” said De Leon, Jr.
After winning 12 straight Mina defeated Argentina’s Gregorio Peralta, 11-2-3, stopping him in 8 rounds. He got up to 16 straight when he fought Humberto Loayza of Chile whom he had defeated 2 months prior to this with this time ending in a draw. Within 30 days Mina was proclaimed South American champion the end of 1960. The following month they had their third meeting with Mina scoring a fifth round knockout.
“Mina’s popularity grows. Newspapers fill page after page. He does television interviews and becomes a national figure. The masses followed him wherever he went because they didn’t just value his athletic achievements. They valued his qualities in and out of the ring. He was always mindful of how he acted. To him everyone was a friend. There were no enemies. He was down to earth. Rich and poor people could call and talk to him.
“Fighters Mina was fighting were like the who’s who of boxing. He was like the Ray Robinson of his hometown. Boxing is no different than any other profession. You’re selling a product and if you have a product like Mina you have no problem because he can handle himself in any situations”, said Dundee. 
After winning 21 straight plus the draw Mina defeated Jesse Bowdry, 28-8, from the US, who had fought Harold Johnson 6 months prior to this for the vacant NBA title. This win put Mina in the NBA ratings at number 10. Mina knocked out Jamaican Allan Harmon, 27-7-3. In the dressing room after the fight Harmon still doesn’t remember the end of the fight due to the right cross from Mina had so much effect on him. “Harmon was a tough young man who fought a draw with Henry Hank in Miami Beach,” said Dundee.
Mina knocked out the number six contender Von Clay, 16-6-2, when Mina was number seven contender. The fight was exciting because Clay hurt Mina with a right cross. But one of Mina’s virtues was his ability to recover. Clay must have thrown 50 punches with only a handful landing. Mina landed a 5 punch combination in the sixth round before Clay dropped to the canvas. The people were ecstatic and applauded him for half an hour after this win. He followed this fight against Cuban Lino Rendon, 16-10-1. Mina was hit with a hard right that he said “temporarily blinded me.” Mina went on to win.
Mina took a trip to Philadelphia in 1962 when NBA champion Harold Johnson was defending against Doug Jones. Mina was introduced in the ring challenging the winner. Johnson won and was offered 50k to come to Lima but turned it down. A month after defeating Jones, Johnson traveled to Germany and defeated the European champion Gustav “Bubi” Scholz, 85-1-6. Johnson once told me Scholz was as good as the American fighters.
This writer only saw Mina fight one time in his only fight in the US in November of 1962 defeating Detroit’s “Hammerin” Henry Hank, 53-16-3, by split decision. Referee Arthur Mercante had it 6-3 while another judge Bill Recht 5-3 both for Mina. Judge Artie Aidala 6-4 for Hank. This writer had it 6-4 for Mina while pulling out those last 2 rounds. Prior to the fight Announcer Don Dunphy called it a carnival like atmosphere with mostly Puerto Ricans supporting Mina.
The matchmaker of the Garden had told Mina’s advisor “he will be the challenger.” In Hank’s previous fight he defeated future heavyweight champion Jimmy Ellis. Hank took the first two rounds before Mina opened up in the third round but Hank came back in taking the fourth. In the fifth a fight broke out with Mina coming out aggressively on top. He also took the sixth and seventh rounds. Hank landed uppercuts in the eighth to take the round. He looked like he thought he was ahead going into the last round as Mina finished the stronger of the two.
The Hank fight was in between a pair of wins over Seattle’s Eddie Cotton, 42-12-1, in Peru. It was marred by a plane crash the day before when 97 people died with little to cheer about when Mina returned from New York.
Cotton was the number one contender but Mina replaced him at that position after defeating him. Cotton agreed to come to Lima Mina was placed face to face with his destiny. The first fight had 32,900 in attendance in October of 1962. The second one had 35,000 in attendance in January of 1963. Previously in August of 1961 Cotton had lost by split decision to NBA world champion Harold Johnson. The winner of the first Cotton-Mina fight was to get a shot at Johnson’s title in Madison Square Garden which was later changed to the Convention Center in Las Vegas, NV.
Cotton brought his trainer, meat and water for this second fight. The second fight was a lot rougher for Mina. His management wanted him to have 3 more fights before challenging for the title. He won them with the last one defeating future champion Bob Foster. “Angelo Dundee sent me down to fight Mina. They didn’t know how tall I was or the puncher I was,” said Foster. Mina suffered a cut over his left eye.
Early in 1963 Mina was to get his title shot but claimed he hurt his right hand with pain from the hand to the elbow that felt like small snakes cancelling his fight with Johnson. He was moved to a private room with a sign saying “Dangerous Crazy Man” to keep the press away. He also had Glaucoma in his left eye. The hospitals doctor denied the eye operation. Mina denied having a problem with his left eye. Johnson would lose his title to Willie Pastrano who filled in for Mina. The Cotton-Mina second fight winner was to get a title fight with Pastrano but when Pastrano lost a non-title fight to Peralta he was obligated to fight him in 1964 retaining the title.
Boxing manager Jim Jacobs told me it was the worst decision he ever saw of the thousands of films he owned saying Johnson won it. Mina went to a hospital after this fight and it was hush-hush what his injury’s from the fight amounted to. Rumors were he had a detached retina. New York physician discovered this on a Mina visit and took away his license as did Peru and the rest of the boxing world. Madison Square Garden’s President John Condon was told by Mina’s former promoter Aguirre about the operation. Aguirre denied the accusation. The physician felt it was a successful operation but despite that it cost the Garden 100k for this cancellation. Mina would have gotten 20k for the fight.
Mina returned to the ring after 8 months and defeated Roque Maravilla, 34-9-1, of the US when the fight fell through between Johnson and Mina. “I would have loved to of had a kid like Mauro Mina. He was the kind of guy people wanted to see. Mauro Mina would have been great at any time,” said Angelo Dundee. The boxer who defeated Pastrano for the championship Jose Torres said, “Mina was a very nice guy, well- mannered and a thinker.”
Historian Kaplan said “Eddie Cotton had great techniques, a classic boxer. He danced well. He used his arms with a mastery that neutralized his rivals. Cotton the painter and Mina the sculptor. Not only poor people went to see Mina fight but from all social classes and Mina represented a national continent and a country like ours that needs triumph in all areas, not just in sports.”
Taking a look back to the beginning of Mina’s career after winning his first 6 fights starting in October of 1955, Mina was ill advised to take on the much more experienced Brazilian champion Luis Ignacio, 22-2-1, losing in Sao Paulo, BRZ. In a rematch in 1958 it ended in a draw, in Peru. In his next fight being just 10-1-1 he traveled to Montevideo, URG, and lost to Dogomar Martinez, 46-2-5, who was the South American champion by a score of 6-4-5. Mina would go onto win 16 straight including Argentine’s Gregorio Peralta, 11-2-3. It included in his first of 3 fights with Humberto Loayza, 37-18-4, of Chile. In their second fight it ended in a draw while Mina won the South American title in their third and last fight scoring a knockout.
In November of 1963 Mina defeated future world champion Bob Foster, 11-1, over 10 rounds. “We hurt each other. When I hurt him they’d ring the bell. I had a few lumps. He was a good fighter and the best I had fought in the light heavyweight division. He would have beaten Pastrano,” said Bob Foster.
Mina would fight Thomas again in Lima ending in a draw though the fight was scheduled for New York originally. Mina’s left eye was shut tight. He would go on a 20 fight win streak before losing in a rematch to Gregorio Peralta, 42-4-4, who was then the South American heavyweight champion in September of 1964. Mina had stopped Peralta when both were light heavyweights in June of 1960. He was 37-0-2 over 39 fights. Mina said he was tired of boxing after this fight. Dr. Francisco Levano of the Boxing Federation advised him to stop fighting because there was no guarantee the eye would be injured again.
Mina’s son said he’d tell us “you discriminate against yourselves sometimes. I won’t go to place’s because they may discriminate against me. He taught us that we’re not different from others. We are all equal.” In 1964 Mina was 31 and his wife Sophia 18 when they married after knowing each other for a year. There were 1,000 people in attendance and another 5,000 outside the church. It caused a negative reaction due to his wife being white by the black women in Mina’s circle. When they left the church Mina had one of his gloves and a hankie from him. They tried to take Sophia’s veil. They would go onto have 3 children. This wedding was marred by a riot during a soccer game between Peru and Argentina that killed 253 people.
Mina ended his career defeating Italy’s champion Piero Del Papa, 28-1-3, before 15,000 in attendance in November of 1965. Del Papa would win the European title in his next fight. He turned professional at the age of 21 and in his last fight he was 31 just weeks before his 32nd birthday. He announced his retirement in April of 1966. He continued with his boxing academy and built several apartments for added income. He taught at a Naval School and trained Peru’s National team and became a successful manager. He passed away at the age of 59 of complications from a stroke in June of 1993. He was known as a “champion without a crown!”
“Mauro Mina would have been a champion in any era. I’m talking about a 60 year span because I’ve been around for 60 years,” said Angelo Dundee.

text:
Just started @Deadtiles and the first hour actually feels like a proper survival game instead of a crypto wallet connector with zombies glued on.

You wake up in Birchport Hospital. Doctor Clark fixed you up. You’re hungry, thirsty, and the world outside is dead.

Here’s exactly what to do in the first session so you don’t look like a complete noob:

1. Walk around (WASD or click the ground on PC, stick/tap on phone)
2. Talk to Doctor Clark, ask what happened, take the work he offers
3. Eat the tuna and drink the water in your pack. Hunger or thirst at zero = you start dying
4. Open the map. Hospital, barracks, and market are marked
5. Leave the ward and report to Captain Davis in the barracks mess hall
6. Read the job before you accept it. That’s how you start earning the National Guard trust

Once the tutorial ends you’re on your own.

Scavenge. Stay fed and warm. Do the work Davis posts. Build somewhere safe. Gear doesn’t carry over if you die with it on you, only skills, standing, and finished jobs do.

Game is free. Browser only. Phantom or Solflare.
https://t.co/zSuXDdd2TR

The Field Guide in your Journal covers the same stuff if you forget.

Trading in Deadtiles is actually one of the cleaner systems I’ve seen in a survival game.

Banknotes are the real currency inside Ashen County.  
Jobs pay notes. Kevin buys your scavenged junk. Other players buy whatever you put on the market board.

Kevin runs the Ashen Traders stall at Birchport market (it’s marked on the map).  
If you’re Hostile or Exiled with them, his counter is closed. No buying, no selling.

His prices depend hard on your standing:

➠ Wary → you pay 200%, he only gives you 10%  
➠ Neutral → normal prices, he pays 20%  
➠ Warm → 95% / 25%  
➠ Friendly → 90% / 30%  
➠ Allied → 80% / 40%

Buying and selling both slowly raise your standing. Bartering skill helps a bit more.

You can also rent a safe deposit box for 1,000 notes. Anything in the box stays safe when you die.

Player market is the other side.  
List stuff for other survivors. Listings last 7 days. If it doesn’t sell, the goods just sit at the desk waiting for you.

The cut only comes out when it sells (not when you list). Allied standing pays 0% cut and can have 30 listings up at once.

Wary only gets 1 listing and 20% cut.  
Hostile/Exiled can’t list at all.

So yeah… your reputation actually matters here. Not just for flavor.

After the earlier private-sale request was denied, Trustee Christina Lovato is proposing competitive bidding for the estate’s claims against Authentix and 24M Technologies.

It’s the buyer whose offer establishes the starting point for other qualified bidders to beat.

“Net” means litigation fees and expenses are deducted before calculating the estate’s share.

The Trustee says pursuing these cases could cost $1.5 million or more. Her approach would preserve estate cash while retaining part of any recovery.

BaileyBridge would fund and control the litigation. Other qualified buyers could submit better offers.

The proposed requirements include a $315,000 minimum deposit, qualified lawyers, at least $1 million available for litigation, and sworn independence and good-faith commitments.

The term sheet requires Trustee consent AND court approval for settlements. Assignment §7.2 instead describes Trustee consultation and court approval. That wording should be reconciled so settlement authority is clear.

Not all grains offer the same nutritional benefits.

Whole grains contain all three parts of the grain: the bran, germ, and endosperm.

Refined grains have the bran and germ removed during processing, which reduces their fiber content and removes some nutrients.

Good sources of whole grains include:
- Oats
- Brown rice
- Whole-wheat bread
- Barley

You don't need to change your entire diet at once. Swapping a refined grain for a whole-grain option now and then is a simple place to start.

👉 A NOTE ON YAMA THARPANA

It is prescribed that, on the day of Naraka Chaturdasi all those who are eligible to offer Pithru tharpana should give Thila Tharpana in the name of Yama Dharma Raja (God of Death) called Yama Tharpana by reciting the following sloka containing 14 names of Yama Dharma Raja.

यमाय धर्मराजाय मृत्यवे चांतकाय च ।
वैवस्वताय कालाय सर्व भूतक्षयाय च ॥
औदुंबराय दध्नाय नीलाय परमेष्ठिने ।
वृकोदराय चित्राय चित्रगुप्ताय वै नमः ॥

yamāya dharmarājāya mṛtyave cāṃtakāya ca |
vaivasvatāya kālāya sarva bhūtakṣayāya ca ||
auduṃbarāya dadhnāya nīlāya parameṣṭhine |
vṛkodarāya citrāya citraguptāya vai namaḥ ||

ಯಮಾಯ ಧರ್ಮರಾಜಾಯ ಮೃತ್ಯವೇ ಚಾಂತಕಾಯ ಚ ।
ವೈವಸ್ವತಾಯ ಕಾಲಾಯ ಸರ್ವ ಭೂತಕ್ಷಯಾಯ ಚ ।।
ಔದುಂಬರಾಯ ದಧ್ನಾಯ ನೀಲಾಯ ಪರಮೇಷ್ಠಿನೇ ।
ವೃಕೋದರಾಯ ಚಿತ್ರಾಯ ಚಿತ್ರಗುಪ್ತಾಯ ವೈ ನಮಃ ।।

యమాయ ధర్మరాజాయ మృత్యవే చాంతకాయ చ |
వైవస్వతాయ కాలాయ సర్వ భూతక్షయాయ చ ||
ఔదుంబరాయ దధ్నాయ నీలాయ పరమేష్ఠినే |
వృకోదరాయ చిత్రాయ చిత్రగుప్తాయ వై నమః ||

1. Yamaya Namah
2. Dharmaraajaya Namah
3. Mruthyave Namah
4. ChAntakaya Namah
5. Vaivaswathaya Namah
6. Kaalaaya Namah
7. Sarva BhoothaKshayaaya Namah
8. Aaudhumbaraaya Namah
9. Dhadnaaya Namah
10. Neelaaya Namah
11. Parameshtine Namah
12. Vrukodaraaya Namah
13. Chitraaya Namah
14. Chitraguptaaya Namah

Facing South,

Tharpana should be given with water and black sesame seeds (thila) with Yagnopaveetham in Savya position from Deva Theetha like Deva Tharpana (Yama Dharma Raaja being a Devatha) by reciting each name in the above sloka by adding Namah.

For example...

Yamaaya Namah >Yamam Tharpayami;
Dharmarajaya Namah > Dharmarajam Tharpayami;

Sacred scripts (Dharma Shastra) says that this Tharpana should be given by one and all irrespective of the fact whether father is alive or not.

In case father is alive (JeEvatpithru) it should be given with water and rice with Yagnopaveetham in Savya position. Thila should not be used in such case.

Why with Thila, facing South and in Savya Position?

·  Thila because Lord Yama has Pithrutva,

·  South because He is the Governing Lord of South direction (Dikkpalaka), and

·  Savya because He is a Devata.

Yamadharma Raja is having both Devatva as well as Pithrutva.

YamaDharmaRaja is a Devatha, one of the Ashta DikkPalakas' governing South (Dakshina) direction; born to Lord Surya & Sa~jna Devi.

Lord Yama has two roles...

As Mrutyu DEvatha He is YAMA whose Bimba Moorthy is Sankarshana roopi Paramatma.

As DHARMA Devata He is DHARMARAJA whose Bimba Moorthy is Bhagawan Sri RamaChandra.

put together He is YAMADHARMARAJA.

YAMA THARPANA on the day of Naraka Chaturdasi and Krishna Angaraka Chaturdasi (Tuesday associated with Chaturdasi during Krishna Paksha) is compulsory.

Apart from the above days, Yama Tharpana is also prescribed during Mahalaya Pithru Paksha and on every Krishna Chaturdasi day during Bahula Paksha.

Vruddha Manuhu Sloka for Yama Tharpana on Naraka Chaturdasi & Krishna Angaraka Chaturdasi.

दीपोत्सव चतुर्दश्यां कार्यां तु यम तर्पणम् ।
कृष्णा०गार चतुर्दश्यामपि कार्यं तदैव वा ॥

ದೀಪೋತ್ಸವ ಚತುರ್ದಶ್ಯಾಂ ಕಾರ್ಯಾಂ ತು ಯಮ ತರ್ಪಣಮ್ ।
ಕೃಷ್ಣಾ೦ಗಾರ ಚತುರ್ದಶ್ಯಾಮಪಿ ಕಾರ್ಯಂ ತದೈವ ವಾ ।।

దీపోత్సవ చతుర్దశ్యాం కార్యాం తు యమ తర్పణమ్ |
కృష్ణా౦గార చతుర్దశ్యామపి కార్యం తదైవ వా ||

dīpotsava caturdaśyāṃ kāryāṃ tu yama tarpaṇam |
kṛṣṇā0gāra caturdaśyāmapi kāryaṃ tadaiva vā ||

text:
In the 1960s, Saskatchewan’s Legislature implemented permanent Daylight Saving Time. Their population was had a higher rate of chronic disease ever since.

In 2019, British Columbia’s premier ran an online survey asking if the public would support ditching the switch with pDST. Permanent Standard Time was not offered. There was no way to prevent multiple survey submissions. Results went over 90% to yes. The premier said they would implement pDST as soon as the US did.

In 2020, Yukon’s premier ran the same survey with the same result, and immediately implemented pDST.

In 2021, Alberta’s Legislature asked voters at the ballot box if they would support pDST. Again pST was not offered. Voters said no.

In the spring of 2026, BC’s premier announced they would no longer wait on the US. pDST would be implemented immediately.

AB’s premier soon followed with an announcement that because BC was implementing pDST, and SK already had it as well, they supposedly would have no other choice but to implement pDST immediately, despite the referendum.

Northwest Territories announced they would follow AB into pDST immediately.

In the summer of 2026, Manitoba’s premier ran an online survey, offering both pDST and pST. pDST won. Implemented immediately.

The western edge of Ontario then faced the prospect of becoming a time zone island (surrounded by different clocks to the east and west) if their clocks were to fall back to Standard Time. They ran surveys, some asking pDST only, some asking pDST and pST. pDST won. Implemented immediately.

text:
A snow gun can be running while the ski slope stays closed. 🎿

A ski area needs more than a patch of white beneath a snow gun before it can open a usable route from the lift to the bottom.

The webcam looks promising, the temperature has dropped below freezing, and another mountain appears to be getting on with it.

Yet the thermometer answers only part of the question.

Snowmakers use a measure called wet-bulb temperature, which combines the air temperature with its moisture.

OpenSnow gives an example of air at 32°F with 25% humidity producing a wet-bulb temperature of 24°F.

Dry air can give the equipment a better opportunity than the ordinary temperature reading suggests.

A temperature on a phone also leaves out the conditions where each machine is working.

A reading near the base does not describe every part of the mountain, and a webcam cannot tell you the humidity beside a particular snow gun.

At Mt. Crescent, a ski area in Iowa, site manager Chris Andrew describes using both movable fan guns and fixed snowmaking equipment, with different operating temperatures.

Wind adds another moving part because its strength and direction affect where the snow goes.

Changing conditions can require more crew attention and adjustments to the operation.

A machine sending snow towards the wrong part of a slope is doing visible work without necessarily building the coverage needed.

Snow collected in piles still needs draining and spreading, while the finished surface needs enough depth for grooming and the traffic that follows.

Coverage also has to connect the useful parts of the route, including the lift access and the runout.

A handsome white section halfway down does little for a skier who cannot reach it or finish the descent.

A cold night followed by warm rain presents a different prospect from several cold days, especially when water, pumping capacity, electricity, staff and time are limited.

For an early-season trip, the useful detail is the terrain that will actually open.

One lift and one run may offer exactly the repeated practice someone wants, while another skier expects a day of exploring.

Read the opening notice for those named lifts and runs before turning a photograph of snow into a plan for the whole mountain.

text:
Completely different history than settling on the East Coast, where copious amounts of ships and people were coming in over the years to settle and develop cities there right along the coast and subsequently inland.

The Oregon Trail was ruthless and western expansionism was a more drawn out process. The Oregon Trail ended roughly around Oregon City (near Portland) and was an important center for land claims and settlement. The Willamette Valley was a very fertile area for agriculture and financial incentives were offered. The coastline, however, is very rugged (although beautiful) and there wasn't an already established transatlantic route (like the East Coast had) for ships to travel for shipping routes/trade/immigration. 

Portland grew as a city (albeit much smaller than big cities on the East Coast) because the Columbia River runs all the way from the Pacific Coast directly into Portland once maritime travel on that side of the country became more of a thing. Seattle followed Portland and became a much bigger city due to the deep-water harbor in the Puget Sound (big seafood industry there) and the Klondike Gold Rush.

So by that time most of the "big cities" in America had already been established. There weren't any economic incentives to develop another major city along the west coast (from Seattle to San Francisco).

📍Key Tithi and Timing Details

📍NARAK CHATURDASHI 2026 I THE STORY BEHIND NARAK CHATURDASHI

🕉️According to Hindu traditions, Narak Chaturdashi is associated with Lord Krishna's victory over Narakasura, a powerful demon king who had imprisoned 16,100 women and spread fear across the three worlds.

When his atrocities became unbearable, Lord Krishna, accompanied by Satyabhama, confronted him in battle.

Satyabhama, regarded as an incarnation of Bhudevi (Mother Earth), played a decisive role in Narakasura's defeat.

Before his death, Narakasura is believed to have requested that his passing be celebrated with lights and joy rather than sorrow.

Lord Krishna granted his wish.

Thus, Narak Chaturdashi became a celebration of liberation, the destruction of evil and the triumph of Dharma.

📍TRADITIONAL PRACTICES TO OBSERVE:

🕉️ 1. DHANTERAS TO BHAI DOOJ REMEDY

🪔 Yama Deepam ( दीपदान ) 
🗓️6 NOVEMEBER TO 11 NOVEMBER

▫️Light a mustard-oil diya outside the home, traditionally facing south.
▫️Offer prayers to Yamaraj for the well-being and longevity of family members.
👉🏻A traditional prayer for protection from untimely death.

2. CHOTI DIWALI / KALI CHAUDAS 
🗓️SATURDAY, 7 NOVEMBER 2026

🪔Deep Daan : 14 Diyas

▫️Light 14 diyas as per family tradition.
▫️Dedicate prayers to Yamaraj and your ancestors.
👉🏻Let every flame represent gratitude, remembrance and the triumph of light over darkness.

🙏🏻Hanuman Upasana

▫️Offer sindoor and jasmine oil to Hanuman Ji, following temple tradition.
▫️Recite Hanuman Chalisa with devotion.
🙏🏻Pray for courage, strength and freedom from obstacles.

3. NARAK CHATURDASHI / ROOP CHAUDAS 
🗓️SUNDAY, 8 NOVEMBER 2026

🪔Abhyanga Snan (Sacred Oil Bath) 🌿
👉🏻Timing: 5:40 AM–6:40 AM.
▫️Begin the morning with a sesame oil massage.
▫️Traditionally, add a little turmeric and Gangajal to the bathing water.
👉🏻This ritual symbolises purification, renewal and the removal of negativity.

📍A REMINDER FOR TONIGHT:

▫️Keep your home clean and illuminated.
▫️Light a diya at the entrance.
▫️Offer prayers to Maa Lakshmi, Lord Krishna and Yamaraj.
▫️Remember your ancestors with gratitude.

text:
In Japan, You Can Leave Your Bad Fortune Behind at a Shrine ⛩️

Imagine receiving a small slip of paper that predicts bad luck.

Most people would probably throw it away.

In Japan, you might tie it to a tree or a special rack at a shrine.

This is part of the tradition of omikuji, written fortunes found at many Shinto shrines and Buddhist temples.

An omikuji may predict great blessings, ordinary luck, or misfortune.

But the message is often more interesting than the ranking.

It may offer advice about health, relationships, work, travel, or the importance of patience.

Visitors sometimes take favorable fortunes home.

Unfavorable ones are often tied at the shrine, expressing a wish to leave misfortune behind or entrust it to the sacred place.

Customs vary by shrine and temple.

What makes omikuji fascinating is that it does not necessarily ask people to surrender to fate.

Even an unfavorable fortune can be read as advice about how to live more carefully.

A small piece of paper cannot control tomorrow.

But it might change how someone approaches it.

Perhaps that is why this centuries-old custom remains so appealing.

It is, therefore, essential to keep the serenity of the judicial process by plac ing it above the cultural, ethnic, religious or personal notions of individual judges. Every judge is accountable to the Constitution and her judgements should reflect this commitment. History reminds us that many judgements by the German courts during the Nazi regime lost their legitimacy after Hitler's debacle in the Second World War )

LAST week, a court in Gujarat's Gandhinagar district imposed the punishment of imprisonment for life term to three persons accused of cow slaughter. It was done under the Gujarat Animal Preservation Act. In the judgement, the court cited Manusmriti and certain Vedic ideas, opining that if the accused are not punished, eventually there will be extinction of 'Gau Mata'.

This is not an isolated case. The Allahabad High Court, in a 2023 judgement, spoke more or less in the same voice. The Lucknow Bench of the court refused to quash a chargesheet prepared under the Uttar Pradesh Prevention of Cow Slaughter Act. The court stated, "In Hinduism, the belief and faith is that cow is a representative of divine and natural beneficence and should therefore be protected and venerated."

In 2017, the Rajasthan High Court issued directives for declaring cow the national animal of India. Justice Mahesh Chandra Sharma issued the direction just one day before his retirement. In 2021, Justice Shekhar Kumar Yadav of the Allahabad High Court also said that the cow must be declared the national animal and its protection must be declared a fundamental right of Hindus. According to the judge, there are scientists who believe that the cow is the only animal that inhales and exhales oxygen!

In yet another episode, in a maintenance case, Justice Praveen Kumar Giri of the Allahabad High Court cited Manusmriti to underline the husband's "pious obligation" to support his wife.

Any court in India is entitled to rely on constitutional or statutory text to justify its conclusion in a case. But often, the judges rely on Puranas and other religious texts, creating a sort of judicial populism that tends to support religious majoritarianism. This is not a healthy development for a secular democracy. While dealing with cases of gender equality or caste, if a constitutional court relies on ancient religious texts instead of constitutional principles, serious problems could arise.

Indian secularism, as explained by the Supreme Court in SR Bommai (1994), is not against religion. Yet, when our courts try to decide cases based on religious text or beliefs, there is an inevitable element of subjectivity and uncertainty in adjudication. For the process to remain constitutional and not ecclesiastical-the judges need to follow adjudicative discipline.

Courts' invocation of religious texts is not an entirely new trend. Judges, who take oath by the Constitution, must place the judicial process above cultural, ethnic or personal notions

In a multi-religious society, it is the Constitution that unites various faiths, ideas, languages and cultures. It is the document by which we resolved to constitute India as a democracy. It is the document that promises and gives lib erty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship. It is the home that offers dignity to every individual and assures equality before the law and equal protection of the laws. The judges of the higher judiciary take oath under this Constitution while assuming charge. and are bound to be faithful to it.

Let it not be, however, misunder stood that such inclinations towards Hindu religious texts is only a recent judicial trend. Scholar Saumya Saxena in a 2018 paper has shown that the Su preme Court's judgements have tried to legitimise the politics of Hindutva

right from the 1990s. She has referred to judgements like Ramesh Yeshwant Prabhoo us Prabhakar Kashinath Kunte (1995) and Manohar Joshi us Nitin Bhaurao Patil (1995). Yeshwant Prabhoo projected Hindutva as "a way of life of the people in the subconti nent". In Manohar Joshi, the Supreme Court said that a call for establishing a Hindu state in Maharashtra in itself did not amount to appealing for votes on the ground of religion.

It is after the publication of Saumya's paper that the five-judge Bench of the Supreme Court decided the Babri Masjid demolition case (M Siddiq us Mahant Suresh Das, 2019). In this, the court directed to convey the disputed land for construction of a temple by a trust to be created by a 'secular' government. It showed the fusion of the State with religion through a process of the court. The rest is history.

What happened in Indian courts along with the rise of Hindutva would indicate an ideological shift, often abetted by the pragmaticism of individual judges. Generally, judges do not go against the tide. The affinity towards Manusmriti and the Puranas indicates an embarrassing extension of such judicial gesture. It is not an issue of language. It is a question of attitude.

But then, the political situation out-side the court is radically altered. The country now witnesses a political praxis that tries to regain her consti tutionalism. Secularism finds its own organic revival, as was evident in some recent protests. With the people's understanding about the damage done to the nation's Constitution, particu-larly by way of electoral manipulation, India has started to regain her consti-tutional vocabulary-one which the courts can no longer ignore.

Let it also be noted that the massive expulsion of voters was not unconnected with religion. Minorities and women were the primary victims of the so-called special revision of electoral rolls in several states. This means that secularism, as an idea, was attacked at the very fundamental level of one-person-one-vote.

This takes us to the foundational question that goes well beyond the judicial language in verdicts. In his 1921 classic, The Nature of the Judicial Proc ess, Benjamin N Cardozo, an associate judge of the US Supreme Court, asked: "What is it that I do when I decide a case? To what sources of information do I appeal for guidance? In what proportions do I permit them to contribute to the result?" In his answer, after not-ing the importance of the Constitution, statutes and precedents, he wrote: "The great generalities of the Constitution have a content and a significance that vary from age to age. The method of free decision sees through the transitory particulars and reaches what is permanent behind them."

It is, therefore, essential to keep the serenity of the judicial process by plac ing it above the cultural, ethnic, religious or personal notions of individual judges. Every judge is accountable to the Constitution and her judgements should reflect this commitment. History reminds us that many judgements by the German courts during the Nazi regime lost their legitimacy after Hitler's debacle in the Second World War. text:
Why did Elon Musk's roughly $470-500 million in 2026 election spending end up making the story that he was trying to buy the election?

Erin Griffith (@eringriffith) and Ezra Klein (@ezraklein) on Hard Fork (@nytimes). What stood out 👇

1. AI is politically toxic because the pitch is bad and the people rolling it out seem untrustworthy
Ezra cites exit polls: 56% said AI and data centers were a major factor in their vote, 57% said AI would hurt society, and 76% opposed a data center nearby. Trump took the Saxs/Andreessen line of “let them rip,” which put Republicans on the wrong side of opinion. Ezra says the basic sell is that AI might kill everyone and probably take your job. Regulation could have built trust.

2. Revealed preferences don’t prove people want AI: heavy usage hasn’t bought public acceptance
Erin says many VCs argue people distrust big tech but love their iPhones, Facebook and Amazon, so ChatGPT’s billion users mean they’ll accept AI too. She thinks this election shows that reading is wrong, since voters were angry enough to reject AI outright. Ezra adds that many AI insiders privately say they would push the pause button but feel it can’t be stopped. Politicians who don’t buy that inevitability want to pace it and regulate it.

3. Data centers were a spiky wedge issue that crossed party lines where the buildout is heaviest
Data centers ranked low in issue polls but won on a yes/no question. Ezra and Erin say they mattered most in states building them: Texas, Ohio, Georgia and Arizona. Democrats hit Ramaswamy and Husted on the issue in Ohio, and it worked as a wedge that won over Republicans. Erin says investors fear 10 to 15 gigawatts of the roughly 45 gigawatts due next year could now be at risk, especially in Texas.

4. A data center slowdown might actually be good for markets by pacing capex to real usefulness
Ezra offers a contrarian take. Markets bounced Wednesday despite investor panic. He suspects a collective-rationality problem in which everyone overinvests in data centers for fear of being left behind. Externally paced capex could weed out fly-by-night players and push Anthropic and OpenAI toward making products economically useful instead of racing to superintelligence. What markets need is alignment between buildout speed and adoption.

5. Musk’s huge spending was counterproductive because it made Elon is trying to buy the election the story
Ezra says the money bought attention, but the attention was that Musk was trying to buy the election, especially in Texas, handing Talarico and others a foil. Teddy says Musk spent roughly $470-500 million, about half of it on Texas and Ken Paxton’s race, and Paxton lost by a lot. Teddy notes Paxton might have lost anyway, so the best ROI may have been not to spend.

6. The California wealth tax failed because of a $330 million fight and state-level flight fears, and it will return nationally
The wealth tax proposition lost despite anti-billionaire sentiment. Erin blames Californians’ fatigue with half-baked propositions. Teddy says Sergey Brin and other tech figures spent $330 million against it while the union-backed side raised little. Ezra thinks a national wealth tax is stronger because billionaires can’t flee the IRS, and expects it to be table stakes for Democrats in 2028.

7. Tech-right politicians like Vance and Ramaswamy “speak Trump with an accent” and can’t win on their own
Ezra says Trump’s cruelty works because he knows where the lines are. Imitators like Ramaswamy, who ended his Ohio campaign by putting his opponent’s mother on TV to call her a liar, are like “a GPT3 level LLM”: smart but with no feel for the situation. The tech right could only be a factional player within a coalition run by Trump’s charisma. Ezra thinks it is fragile because it doesn’t seem to like or listen to ordinary people.

8. Tech has no positive political story now, because AI is seen first as a threat, not a messaging problem
Ezra contrasts today with the 2008 era, when tech meant the internet and green energy. Now tech means AI, and for most people the answer to “do we want this?” is “not under these conditions.” No politician will run on wanting far more AI. He says the problem is that the future on offer, humans as well-kept pets of superintelligence, is not one people want. Erin and Max expect a normal CEO like Nadella to be the safe play.

9. Political money was a mixed bet: Hoffman and Brin won, while crypto and AI donors hit limits
Teddy ranks Reed Hoffman and Brin at the top. Hoffman put $17 million behind Talarico, who won big. Fairshake spent $45 million against Sherrod Brown, who won. Greg Brockman’s family pledged $50 million to Leading the Future but only gave $25 million, partly because the PAC became a distraction. Meta pulled back $20-25 million of state giving. People feel more strongly about AI than about crypto, so AI money is riskier.

10. AI-safety money and dark money will shape 2028, and nobody can see most of it
Teddy says the AI-safety donor base around Anthropic is a large source of cash and will be a force in the Democratic primary. Anthropic’s IPO could mint many civic-minded donors, and Democratic fundraisers are watching. Teddy also cautions that disclosure is falling, with money flowing through newly created nonprofits, especially on the Democratic side where donors fear Trump retaliation. Teddy expects Musk to back Vance in the 2028 Republican primary.

text:
An engineer can justify a $100,000 yearly AI token budget. A lawyer or CFO gets $200 to $2,000 a month. Investors still can't name what comes after coding.

Biggest takeaways on TBPN (@tbpn) new episode:

1. The selloff is a post-midterm repricing of the data center buildout, hitting chip and neocloud names hardest while hyperscalers hold up.
The hosts say the Nasdaq fell 5% into correction territory and the S&P 500 had its worst day since April 2025. Investors are positioning for an easing in the data center buildout, with some chip and power names down 50–60%. The hosts note most of the big Mag Seven are down only about 2%, because their data centers are already built and can be reconfigured. Neoclouds look more exposed.

2. The AI bear question is “what comes after AI coding?” because spend outside engineering is capped at a few hundred dollars a month.
Citing Joe Wisenthal, the hosts say investors can’t name the next engine of ARR after coding. An engineer can justify a $100,000 yearly token budget against a $200–400K compensation package, and Jensen floated a 1:1 ratio. A lawyer, marketer or CFO is offered $200 to maybe $2,000 a month, not $20,000, because ROI isn’t proven there. They say the market needs a real step up in capability.

3. AI for science can still be financed early because markets price breakthroughs before they diffuse, as with GLP-1s.
The hosts argue that drug and chip-design breakthroughs face slow adoption, since regulators want a phase three trial showing a human took the pill and survived a year later. But the market capitalized on GLP-1s, which “drove a trillion dollars of market cap” while rollouts were still very limited. They think some financing could be underwritten by expected AI-for-science breakthroughs, matching capital to long timelines.

4. Anthropic’s IPO may need a discount, but the hosts say a cut would still leave investors in the green.
Jim Cramer says Anthropic will have to take a discount. The hosts note the last round was about $960 billion, so even an IPO at $1.2 trillion is an up-round, and a 50% haircut from the $2 trillion hype still leaves holders in profit. Prediction market odds of an IPO before December 1 fell from 88% to about 61%. The open question is whether to list while the whole supply chain is selling off. Retail may get more allocation.

5. Data center exposure in Texas and local pushback are the next risk, and a $500 million loan portfolio is up for auction.
Cramer flags Texas sites at Iren and CoreWeave, while Nebius has less Texas exposure. Analysts will dig into permits and possible pauses or renegotiations. Bloomberg reports an anonymous seller is auctioning about $500 million of data center loans, including a $25 million slice tied to the Stargate site in New Mexico, where Oracle cited force majeure. Bids are due November 19, with a $10 million minimum.

6. Take-Two answers the one big hit worry with its portfolio of owned IP, and GTA 6 is two grand slams at once.
CEO Strauss Zelnick points to 15 franchises that each sold at least 5 million units, plus Red Dead Redemption, NBA 2K and others. The hosts concede GTA is a power-law outlier. They say it has to land both as a polished single-player game and as an online economic engine like GTA Online. Take-Two was up about 10% over five days while the market sank.

7. Greg Brockman says OpenAI’s rough first half turned into a Q3 revenue inflection as agentic coding took off.
Per the Wall Street Journal interview, Anthropic pulled ahead with business customers early in the year. In Q3, OpenAI’s agentic coding tools found traction and enterprise overtook consumer. The hosts say Brockman pointed to over 100% quarter-on-quarter enterprise growth, while Anthropic’s decelerated to around 49%, as proof of share gains. He credits the GPT 5.6 release.

Morgan Stanley Views Tesla’s Cybertruck Production Scale-Back as a Positive Signal for Its Robotaxi Business

On November 6, Morgan Stanley offered a positive assessment of Tesla’s strategy to scale back Cybertruck production and expand Cybercab manufacturing capacity.

Elon Musk announced plans to gradually wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas starting in mid-2027, reallocating production capacity to increase Cybercab output.

Morgan Stanley interpreted this decision as a sign of Tesla’s growing confidence in the long-term potential of its Robotaxi business.

Several key points stand out:

- Strategic Production Shift: Tesla is prioritizing Cybercab, a potential long-term growth driver, over the Cybertruck, which has faced weaker-than-expected demand.

- Manufacturing Capacity: Tesla plans to leverage its existing Giga Texas infrastructure to support higher Cybercab production volumes.

- Robotaxi Expansion: Progress in Austin’s Robotaxi operations, combined with the potential deployment of Cybercab vehicles, could support future production growth.

- Long-Term Growth Strategy: Tesla is increasingly shifting its focus from traditional electric vehicle sales toward autonomous mobility services.

This decision reflects both the challenges facing Cybertruck demand and Tesla’s strategic commitment to positioning Cybercab as a cornerstone of its future business.

I urge Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and lawmakers from both parties to use the rainy day fund, which holds about $28.5 billion, to fund most of a high-speed rail line between Houston and Dallas instead of sending every Texan a $1,500 check. A $1,500 check would help my household right now, but it gets spent in a month. High-speed rail would serve Texans for generations.

Per Amtrak, the first line from Houston to Dallas would cost at least $30 billion. Once it’s built, it could be the start of a Texas Triangle high-speed rail system.

I also urge Senator-elect James Talarico to push for federal funding to cover the rest of the Houston–Dallas line and to help start building the rest of the Texas Triangle.

High-speed rail would greatly benefit all Texans. It would get people between Houston and Dallas in about 90 minutes, save travelers money on gas compared with driving, take cars off I-45, use up to 6 times less energy per passenger than flying, and produce about a third of the carbon emissions of a domestic flight. Modern high-speed trains are also built with level boarding and wheelchair space, opening up travel for Texans with disabilities.

Landowners along the route shouldn’t be bullied or lowballed. They should be treated fairly and offered fair compensation for their land, with eminent domain used only as a last resort. Treating landowners fairly isn’t just right; it’s how this project finally gets built.

text:
The $6.4 Billion Fall Guy: Why Blaming North Korea for Binance’s Hack Is Too Easy

Scapegoat in Pyongyang: How the "State Hacker" Myth Excuses Big Crypto Breaches

Did North Korea Really Rob Binance—Or Did We Just Buy the Narrative?

Whenever a catastrophic cyber heist occurs, the public discourse follows a familiar routine. Within hours of Binance losing an unprecedented $6.43 billion on October 29, 2026, western intelligence agencies and blockchain analytics firms announced their verdict: North Korea’s elite unit, TraderTraitor (Lazarus Group), did it.

Case closed? Not so fast.

Ask any cybersecurity professional when there is a high profile hack, they are trained to look past rapid public relations pushes and analyze systemic evidence. When you strip away the headline assertions and examine the technical operational environment of late 2026, the official attribution reads less like ironclad forensic truth and more like a convenient geopolitical script.

Here is why a skeptical analyst should question the reflexive framing that Pyongyang pulled off the largest crypto heist in history.

1. The Democratization of Attack Vectors: Anyone Can Buy or Build This Flow

The official narrative depicts a complex, multi-month campaign: poisoning a developer’s AI coding tool installer in June, running fake executive video interviews in September to drop malware, and using an internal AI tool to harvest credentials by October.

To the non-technical public, this sounds like the exclusive domain of a military-grade nation-state. To anyone working in modern IT security, it sounds like Tuesday.

We live in an era where open-source Large Language Models (LLMs), AI-driven voice/video deepfakes, and automated exploit frameworks are accessible to anyone with a browser. You no longer need a state department budget to run convincing multi-stage social engineering campaigns. A small, highly technical squad—whether operating out of Eastern Europe, South America, or a Western tech hub—could easily orchestrate this pipeline.

By labeling every sophisticated attack "state-sponsored," the security industry creates a dangerous myth: that commercial criminal syndicates or rogue internal developers are incapable of advanced execution.

2. The "Commingled Funds" Trap: Framing via Public Blockchain Laundering

The primary evidence offered by analytics firms to link Binance’s stolen billions to North Korea is "on-chain commingling." They point out that automated laundering scripts moved stolen funds into wallet clusters previously associated with earlier heists, such as the September 2026 Bitget hack.

However, relying strictly on wallet overlap for attribution ignores basic operational counter-intelligence: False Flag operations.

Crypto laundering infrastructure is not a physical building with a national flag outside. It consists of public mixer protocols, decentralized exchanges, and automated laundering scripts. If a non-state syndicate wanted to pull off a $6.4 billion heist and ensure global law enforcement pointed their radar in the wrong direction, what would they do? They would intentionally route a fraction of their loot through known, blacklisted DPRK-linked addresses.

In the security world, burning a small percentage of your stolen capital to buy total attribution misdirection isn't a mistake—it is brilliant operational security (OPSEC).

3. The Money Laundering Machine: Automated Infrastructure is Commodity Software

Advocates of the state narrative argue that processing 65,000 transactions across 16 blockchains at a rate of one transaction every 10 seconds requires state-level machinery.

In reality, running automated cross-chain scripts is simple software engineering. Any competent developer can write a Python script utilizing standard Web3 libraries to split funds into thousands of temporary wallets, route them through decentralized protocols like Uniswap or SunSwap, and push them into Wasabi-style coinjoins.

Southeast Asian gambling and scam syndicates already handle multi-billion-dollar international money movement annually. 

Combined with modern, AI-assisted coding tools, a criminal syndicate possesses every piece of infrastructure necessary to execute high-velocity, programmatic laundering without ever setting foot in Pyongyang.

4. Institutional Accountability vs. The Sovereign Boogeyman

Attributing cyberattacks to North Korea offers a massive strategic benefit to corporate targets and regulatory bodies: Absolution.

If an exchange loses billions to a local criminal ring, a rogue insider, or basic corporate negligence, the fallout is devastating. Questions immediately turn to internal access controls, key management, and institutional liability.

However, if the culprit is branded as a "nuclear-armed, state-sponsored super-hacker unit," the framing transforms instantly. The exchange shifts from a negligent corporation into a victim of an act of cyber-warfare. Regulatory pressure softens, insurance claims move smoother, and public outrage is redirected toward a foreign geopolitical adversary that will never respond to a subpoena or appear in a Western courtroom.

Conclusion: We Need Audits, Not Allegations
None of this proves that North Korea didn't play a role in the Binance breach. They remain a formidable threat actor with a documented history in digital asset theft.

However, accepting "TraderTraitor" as the definitive culprit within hours of the breach—based on reusable laundering scripts and commingled public wallet trails—sets a troubling precedent. It ignores the reality of democratized AI tools, disregards the possibility of deliberate false-flag routing, and excuses corporate security failures under the guise of geopolitical inevitability.

Until independent security auditors receive full access to raw endpoint logs, internal AI telemetry, and unredacted forensic data, we should treat the official narrative for what it is: an educated guess wrapped in political convenience.

text:
I drove home and knocked on the door of the oldest person on the street, Louise Marchetti, who was eighty-three and had watched me mow my lawn badly for two years. I showed her the film.

She read it with a magnifying glass and didn't say anything for a while.

"Emil," she said. "That's Emil's coat."

Emil Sorensen was the man who had owned my house. He had worked as a draftsman for the state, she told me, and in the spring of 1968 he saw the plan before anyone was supposed to. He copied it on his lunch hour and walked it down the street, house to house, saying the road was coming.

Nobody believed him. A state employee, with a roof over his own head, telling people their homes would be gone? Half the street thought he was after their lots. Some took low offers from the department and left. The rest only came around when the survey stakes appeared in their yards.

By then the department had worked out who had leaked it. He was fired. He spent the next thirty years drawing kitchen remodels for a lumber yard.

"And the circle?" I asked.

"He circled his own house first," Louise said. "He told us, 'Look. It's mine too.' I didn't understand what he meant until just now."

She said the neighborhood never thanked him. The people who fought hardest were the ones who'd been angriest at him, and after the road died, nobody knew how to bring it up. He kept the film in his coat pocket for fifty years. It was the only proof he hadn't lied.

I gave the strip to the county historical society, but first I had Joyce print the frame with my street on it. Louise hung it in her kitchen, next to the window that looks at my house.

I'd spent a night believing that circle meant my home was in danger. It was a man putting his own house at risk first, so that the rest of us would get the chance to keep ours.

text:
“New York is a land of near horizons, lifting high-angled screens between its folded valleys. Its days are full of clouds that drift over green summits and cast effervescent figures on tilted fields, of sunny elms inexorably darkened by the march of shadow from straight-edged slopes. In these halls, the Onondaga kept their sacred fires, interpreting to the Iroquois nations the message of the Creator and those of the warrior who found paradise at the end of the right fork of the Milky Way. And when the Indians had been exiled by the white pioneers, they would raise their eyes to the earthen walls of their cleared lands and find spiritual release above them in those starry reaches where men have often fancied the gods walked.

And so it happens that in almost every little land today, people tell the story of someone who saw visions few may see, a voice meant only for pointed ears. The little winds that wander the labyrinth of New York State valleys sometimes bring with them, however, a sound that is not a voice. It is the beat of a drum. The roar of the cities overwhelms it, but there are a few upstate farmers who have not, at some time or another, heard that faraway tattoo. Among the Finger Lakes to the west, the sound is greater still, so loud, in fact, that it is sometimes mistaken for firearms. I have heard the professors of universities and colleges in the region speculate learnedly on the causes that underlie the Guns of Cayuga, but none have given an explanation any more reasonable than that offered by an old fisherman who said, ‘It’s the sound of drums beneath the water.’

Perhaps Chief Jesse Cornplanter of the Seneca Nation was right when he told me, ‘The New York State drums are the death drums of my people. When the British fought the colonies, my forefather, Chief Cornplanter, was a friend of General Washington. But many of the tribe joined with the English armies in fighting against the white man who had taken their land from them. And so, towards the end of the war, the American Congress sent a revenging army against the Seneca and the other Iroquois nations. They destroyed our villages, they burned our granaries filled with harvest, they killed our women and children. When they had gone, the Seneca who were left, starving and homeless, beat on their water drums and sang their death songs. Now the drummers are dead too, but sometimes they come back to the places where their villages were and beat their drums again, and sing the death songs for the Senecas killed by the cruel white army.”

—Carl Carmer, Listen for a Lonesome Drum

text:
🇺🇲 🇮🇷 Vance pushes for Iran deal as U.S. military action continues

Vice President JD Vance has spent the past two weeks personally involved in indirect talks with Iran aimed at securing a new ceasefire and restarting nuclear negotiations, Axios reported Friday, citing two sources with knowledge of the matter.

The effort follows Vance's public assertion that the Iran war caused Republicans' midterm defeat. According to Axios reporter Barak Ravid, Vance has spoken almost daily with Qatar's prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, and other mediators. Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are also involved.

Axios reported that Vance sent a letter two weeks ago to Iranian Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei proposing renewed direct negotiations. Iranian officials said the letter generated positive momentum.

The next step remains uncertain. Vance and the mediators have discussed a possible working-level technical meeting between American and Iranian representatives, but it had not materialized, according to Axios. The vice president's office declined to comment.

President Trump offered a brief public signal Friday: "We're talking to them," he told reporters. U.S. officials and regional sources told Axios that Trump was willing to let diplomacy proceed for now, while American forces remained ready to resume strikes on short notice.

Qatar's prime minister said Friday that officials in Washington had a "genuine intention" to contain and de-escalate the situation. He said talks continued after the midterms, although engagement had become less active, and maintained that an agreement was possible.

Qatar's Amiri Diwan separately confirmed a Friday telephone call between Trump and Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani. The emir stressed continued dialogue, diplomatic resolution of differences, freedom of maritime navigation and the security of energy supplies.

Military action continued alongside those contacts. Axios reported that U.S. forces struck an anti-aircraft missile launcher on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday. According to the account reported by Axios, the launcher had fired toward an American fighter jet, and Trump confirmed the U.S. strike.

No new ceasefire has been announced. The diplomatic effort is active, but a technical meeting remains unconfirmed and military exchanges continue around the Strait of Hormuz.
