text:
Harry felt a sudden urge to reach for her hand, to say something, anything that might make this easier for her. But he stopped himself. Even he wasn't daft enough to miss what she was trying to do. She wanted to stand beside him without depending on his friends' loyalty to him, and if he spoke on her behalf now, he would only be giving her another excuse to retreat behind the familiar lies she had spent so long telling herself.
So Harry remained silent, though he could scarcely take his eyes off her.
Ron and Hermione exchanged a glance. Neither seemed quite certain how to respond, and for several seconds, the only sound came from the crackling fire between them.
Finally, Hermione looked up. "Malfoy, I'll be blunt with you. I can't accept your apology, and I'm not ready to forgive you. I'd be lying if I said otherwise."
Draceana's eyes fell to the ground. She had expected that answer, but hearing it still hurt. She said nothing.
"Yeah," Ron agreed, looking rather uncomfortable himself. "Same here. We've had six years of this, haven't we? Can't expect us to forget all that in one night."
Hermione nodded, although her expression softened. "But... I can't believe I'm saying this, but I do believe you meant what you said."
"Never thought I'd hear Malfoy apologize to us," Ron admitted. "Not like that, anyway."
He glanced toward Harry, who remained unusually quiet, then back at Draceana.
"Look, Malfoy. Harry can fancy whoever he likes. Doesn't mean Hermione and I have to agree with him about everything." Ron shifted in his seat. "But you did well at Gringotts. Better than either of us expected, I reckon. Turns out you're not all bark after all."
For once, there was no mockery in his voice. Draceana raised her eyes toward him but remained silent.
"And we're going to need all the help we can get at Hogwarts," Ron continued. "So as far as I'm concerned, you're free to tag along."
Hermione glanced at him, a small smile touching her lips. "I agree," she said. "And not simply because Harry wants you here. You've helped us when we needed it, Malfoy. I think we'd be rather unfair not to acknowledge that."
Draceana looked between them, searching their faces for any sign of reluctance. There was no trace of dishonesty in either Ron's or Hermione's eyes, nor had they stopped to ask what Harry thought. Their answer was theirs alone.
They hadn't forgiven her. She understood that much. But they were willing to have her beside them. That was all Draceana had wanted.
"Thank you," she whispered.
Hermione watched her for another moment before speaking again.
"And Malfoy?"
Draceana looked up.
"If we make it through all this, you can always try again." Hermione offered her a small smile. "Perhaps we'll have a different answer for you then."
Ron gave a small nod in agreement with Hermione's words.
Something in Draceana's expression softened. For once, she couldn't think of a single thing to say. She simply nodded, her lips trembling into the faintest of smiles.
Then, almost without warning, her legs seemed to lose their strength.
"Easy." Harry caught her as she sank back down beside him, wrapping an arm around her shoulders to steady her. Draceana leaned against him, the tension that had held her upright finally giving way to exhaustion.
"Draceana? You all right?" he asked quietly.
She nodded, though her heart was still pounding.
Harry looked down at her, and for a moment, he found himself remembering the girl who had once sneered at him aboard the Hogwarts Express, who would rather have swallowed her own wand than admit she was wrong. But what he'd witnessed tonight was different. No one had forced her to apologize. She hadn't done it to escape punishment or win an argument. She had simply decided, of her own accord, to do what she knew was needed.
Harry smiled and drew her a little closer, his hand resting gently against her shoulder. There was so much he wanted to tell her, but looking at her now, he decided it could wait. This was something she had accomplished herself, and he was proud of the girl he had chosen to love.
Draceana raised her head and met his gaze. Whatever she saw in his expression brought a small smile to her lips, and she settled against him once more, feeling the last of the tension leave her shoulders. She was glad that Harry had opened the door to her cage. And she was even more grateful that she had taken the first step out of it herself. Now, perhaps more than ever, she finally felt she could face her past.
******
The first light of dawn was beginning to spread across the sky when the four of them finally prepared to leave. Their campfire had been extinguished, their belongings packed away, and the riverbank where they had spent the night was slowly disappearing beneath the morning mist. Harry took one last look at their makeshift campsite before turning toward the others.
"We can't Apparate directly into Hogwarts," Hermione reminded them as they gathered together. "The enchantments around the castle won't allow it. We'll have to go through Hogsmeade."
"And once we're there, we get under the Invisibility Cloak," Harry added, pulling the folded silvery fabric from his bag. "We don't know who's watching the village, so let's not take any chances."
"Are you sure you don't want to hold the wand, Potter?" Draceana asked, holding it out to him.
Harry glanced at the wand, then at the cloak in his hands. "I'll need both hands to get this over everyone. You'd better hang on to it for now." He gave her a reassuring smile. "I trust you."
Draceana hesitated before nodding and securing the wand inside her pocket.
Ron eyed the cloak doubtfully. "Four of us under that thing? We'll be tripping over each other!"
"Better that than being spotted," Hermione replied. She reached for his hand and turned toward the others. "Come on, everyone. Concentrate on Hogsmeade."
Harry took Draceana's hand while Ron tightened his grip on Hermione's. They exchanged one last glance, making certain everyone was ready. Then, with their destination fixed firmly in mind, they turned on the spot.
The riverbank vanished.
Harry felt the familiar, unpleasant pressure of Apparition closing around him, squeezing the breath from his lungs before releasing him just as suddenly. His feet struck uneven ground, and he stumbled forward, nearly colliding with Draceana. Cold morning air rushed into his chest as the world steadied around him.
They had arrived on the outskirts of Hogsmeade. A narrow road led toward the village, where familiar rooftops rose beyond the mist, their chimneys silhouetted against the pale morning sky. Hogwarts lay farther beyond, hidden from view by the surrounding hills.
"We made it," Harry breathed.
Ron bent forward, one hand pressed against his stomach. "Merlin, I hate doing that. Doesn't matter how many times—"
"Ron, later," Hermione interrupted. She was already looking around, her expression tense. "Harry, the cloak. Quickly."
Harry nodded and began unfolding it, but before he could raise the silvery fabric over their heads, a shrill, unnatural wailing erupted somewhere within the village.
All four froze.
"What the bloody hell was that?" Ron demanded.
Another wail answered the first, followed by a distant shout. From the direction of the rooftops, a dark shape emerged through the morning mist, then another, their ragged cloaks trailing behind them as they glided above the road.
Harry felt the temperature drop. "Dementors."
"Already?" Hermione looked toward the approaching figures in disbelief. "But we only just arrived!"
"There must be some sort of alarm," Draceana said, her eyes following the creatures as they changed direction toward them. "They know we're here."
Harry glanced at the cloak still hanging from his hands. Getting all four of them underneath it would be difficult enough without Dementors descending upon them.
"Can we outrun them?" Hermione asked.
"Not under this thing," Harry answered, quickly stuffing the cloak back into his bag. "There are too many of us."
"Then forget the cloak!" Ron seized Hermione's hand. "Run!"
They hurried down the road toward Hogsmeade, their footsteps pounding against the damp earth before reaching the village's cobblestones. Harry kept Draceana close beside him, glancing over his shoulder as the Dementors swept after them. The creatures were gaining rapidly, gliding effortlessly above the road while the four teenagers struggled to maintain their pace.
The first houses appeared on either side of them, their windows dark and their doors firmly shut. There was no sign of anyone willing to help, and the morning mist seemed to thicken as the Dementors drew nearer.
Harry could feel their presence now. The cold was sinking through his clothes, making every breath increasingly difficult. Somewhere in the back of his mind, he heard the familiar echoes of screaming, and he shook his head fiercely.
Then, behind him, came a sudden thud.
Harry turned to find Ron sprawled across the cobblestones, having tripped over something in the uneven road and accidentally dragged Hermione down with him. Both struggled to regain their footing as the Dementors swept toward them.
Harry immediately turned to run back, but Draceana was already moving. She rushed past him and placed herself between the fallen pair and the approaching creatures, drawing her wand without a word.
"Draceana!" Harry called as he ran toward them. "The Patronus Charm! Use it!"
She nodded and raised her wand, desperately searching for a happy memory. Her thoughts turned to the moments she treasured most.The happier days with her family, and the precious time she had spent with Harry.Holding on to those memories, she pointed her wand at the approaching Dementors.
"Expecto Patronum!"
A thin stream of silvery light burst from her wand, briefly illuminating the mist. For an instant, it seemed to gather into something brighter, but the light faltered and dissolved before it could take shape.
Draceana blinked in confusion. What?
The Dementors drew closer, and the cold became almost unbearable. Draceana tightened her grip on her wand and tried again, reaching for the same memories. Yet something was wrong. The memories were still there, but the happiness that accompanied them seemed strangely distant. The harder she tried to hold on to it, the further it slipped away.
No, come on...
"Expecto Patronum!"
Another flicker of silver appeared, weaker than the first, and vanished almost immediately.
"I… I can't! I don't understand," she gasped, staring at her wand in disbelief.
"Malfoy, forget it! We've got to run!" Ron shouted, pulling Hermione to her feet.
"Then move your arse already, Weasley!" Draceana snapped, keeping her wand trained on the approaching Dementors.
Harry finally reached them. "Get up, Ron!" he shouted, grabbing his friend's arm and helping him and Hermione to their feet.
His eyes darted toward Draceana. Who had casted the patronus charm twice now to no avail. Why?
Before he could give it another thought, a Dementor swept toward them, its skeletal hand reaching out from beneath its cloak.
Harry quickly seized the wand from Draceana's hand.
"Harry—!" Draceana exclaimed, startled by the sudden movement.
But Harry had already stepped forward. Raising the wand toward the approaching Dementor, he shouted at the top of his lungs.
"EXPECTO PATRONUM!"
A brilliant silver stag burst from the tip of the wand, its antlers shining as it charged straight into the approaching Dementors. The creatures recoiled, scattering above the rooftops as the Patronus drove them back. The terrible cold began to loosen its grip, and Harry could finally breathe properly again.
"Come on!" he shouted, grabbing Draceana's hand.
She hurried after him, still shaken by what had happened, while Ron and Hermione followed close behind.
They had barely taken another step when a rough voice called from somewhere ahead.
"Potter! Over here, you idiot!"
Harry turned sharply. An elderly man with a long grey beard stood in the doorway of the Hog's Head, waving impatiently at them. His face was stern, his clothes rather shabby, and there was something strangely familiar about his piercing blue eyes.
"Unless you fancy getting yourselves killed, get inside!"
Harry pulled Draceana toward the doorway, with Ron and Hermione following close behind. The old man ushered them upstairs before returning to deal with the Death Eaters gathering outside. Through the floorboards, they could hear his furious complaints about being disturbed at such an ungodly hour, followed by an argument that ended with the unwelcome visitors reluctantly departing.
Only when the danger had passed did their rescuer return. Harry recognized him as Aberforth Dumbledore, the younger brother of their late headmaster, although the resemblance did little to soften the man's gruff manner. He was plainly unhappy about their arrival and made no attempt to conceal his opinion of their chances of surviving another encounter with Voldemort's followers.
Harry explained that they needed to enter Hogwarts on a mission Dumbledore had entrusted to him. Aberforth was reluctant to help, warning them that the castle was heavily guarded and that they would be better off abandoning the whole business. But Harry refused to reconsider, and after a brief, increasingly heated exchange, the old man finally relented.
With a weary sigh, Aberforth approached a large portrait hanging above the fireplace. It depicted a young, fair-haired girl whose pale face and gentle expression bore a faint resemblance to the Dumbledore brothers.
He spoke quietly to the girl in the painting. She gave him a small smile before turning away and walking into the darkness behind her, disappearing along what appeared to be a tunnel painted into the canvas.
The four watched in puzzlement.
"Where's she going?" Ron asked.
"To fetch someone," Aberforth answered shortly. "If you're determined to get yourselves into that castle, you'll need a guide."
Several minutes passed before movement appeared in the distant darkness of the portrait. The girl was returning, and behind her came another figure, growing steadily larger as they approached.
Harry leaned forward, squinting at the familiar face. "Hang on..."
The portrait swung open, revealing a real passageway behind the wall. Standing at its entrance was a boy with a battered face, untidy hair, and several bruises that looked painfully recent.
For a moment, Harry could scarcely believe his eyes. "Neville?"
Neville Longbottom broke into a broad grin. "Harry!"
"Neville, look at you!" Harry exclaimed, his smile faltering as he took in the bruises covering his friend's face. "What happened?"
"Oh, this?" Neville touched his swollen cheek and shrugged. "It's nothing, Harry. You should see Seamus." He grinned, looking Harry up and down. "Although, I could say the same about you. All three of you look like you've had better... days."
He stopped.
Neville's gaze had wandered from Harry to Ron, then Hermione, before finally settling on the fourth person standing behind them. His grin disappeared almost immediately.
For a moment, he simply stared, as though unable to believe what he was seeing.
"Hang on." His eyes narrowed. "Malfoy?"
Draceana shifted uncomfortably beneath his stare.
Neville looked back at Harry. "Harry, what's she doing here?"
"She's with me, Neville," Harry answered.
"With you?" Neville repeated incredulously. He glanced between them. "Harry, that's Draceana Malfoy! Are you sure she hasn't hexed you or something?"
"How amusing," Draceana remarked dryly, folding her arms. "Lovely to see you too, Longbottom. Thomas said practically the same thing."
"Draceana, you're not helping," Harry muttered.
She opened her mouth to retort, but stopped herself.
Harry was right. Only hours ago, she had promised herself she would stop running from her past, yet here she was, answering the very first person who questioned her presence with the same contempt she had shown him for years. She could hardly blame Neville for being
suspicious. Apparently, facing her past was going to be much harder than she'd imagined. Harder, perhaps, than repairing that blasted Vanishing Cabinet.
Draceana pressed her lips together and lowered her arms, swallowing whatever remark had been waiting on her tongue.
Harry turned back to Neville, whose expression remained doubtful. He could hardly blame him, to be honest. But there was no time to explain the circumstances that had brought Draceana to his side, nor was this the place to try.
"Listen, Neville, I know how this looks. I'll explain everything once we're inside, I promise. But we really need to get moving. The Death Eaters could be here any minute."
Neville studied Harry for a moment, then glanced once more at Draceana. Whatever questions he had were clearly not going away, but after a brief hesitation, he gave a reluctant nod.
"All right. Only because you say so, Harry." His tone was firm, though his suspicion hadn't entirely disappeared.
Neville stepped aside, allowing the others to enter the passage. Ron and Hermione went first, followed by Harry, who reached back to take Draceana's hand. She cast one last uneasy glance at Neville before following him into the darkness.
Neville watched her pass without another word. Then he followed them into the passage, leaving the portrait to swing shut behind them.
Neville watched her pass without another word. Then he followed them into the passage, leaving the portrait to swing shut behind them.
As they made their way through the passage, Neville explained what had happened at Hogwarts in their absence. Since Snape's appointment as headmaster, the school had become almost unrecognizable. The Death Eaters brought in to teach alongside him were particularly vicious, punishing students for the slightest acts of disobedience and making examples of anyone who dared to resist. Neville spoke of these things with a surprising calmness, as though the cruelty had become an ordinary part of school life. Listening behind Harry, Draceana shifted uncomfortably. She knew perfectly well whose side those people were on, and hearing what they had done to the students made the prospect of facing them even more difficult.
Fortunately, Neville and the others had found a way to resist. He explained that when the Carrows began targeting him, he had desperately needed somewhere to hide, and the Room of Requirement had appeared once again, just as it had when Harry first organized Dumbledore's Army in their fifth year. Since then, Neville had gathered other students who needed refuge, turning the room into a sanctuary where they could rest, recover, and continue their resistance without fear of being discovered.
Neville also revealed that he had already used the enchanted Galleons to alert the other members of Dumbledore's Army. Word of Harry's return would be spreading even now, although he had made certain to mention that Harry wasn't arriving alone. His brief glance toward Draceana made it clear whom he meant. The news would eventually reach the Order of the Phoenix as well, and Neville expected more people to join them before long.
Hermione was visibly impressed by everything Neville had accomplished. She praised his resourcefulness and courage, particularly for keeping Dumbledore's Army together while Harry, Ron, and she had been away. Neville seemed almost embarrassed by the compliment, brushing it aside with a modest smile. As far as he was concerned, he had merely been putting into practice what Harry had taught them all those years ago. Hearing that, Harry couldn't help feeling a quiet swell of pride. The uncertain boy who had once struggled through their Defence Against the Dark Arts lessons was now helping lead the resistance against Voldemort's followers.
Their conversation continued as the passage gradually sloped upward, until at last Neville slowed his pace. Ahead of them, the narrow tunnel opened toward a faint glow of light.
The passage finally opened into the Room of Requirement, and Harry found himself stepping into a vast chamber filled with hammocks, mismatched furniture, and familiar Hogwarts banners hanging from the walls. Nearly two dozen students were gathered inside, some sitting together in small groups while others rested on their makeshift beds. There were Gryffindors, Ravenclaws, and Hufflepuffs, faces Harry recognized from his years at Hogwarts alongside younger students he barely knew. But the moment he emerged from the passage, every conversation seemed to stop.
For a heartbeat, the room fell silent. Then someone shouted his name.
"Harry!"
"Harry Potter!"
"Ron! Hermione!"
The silence shattered into cheers. Students scrambled to their feet, abandoning whatever they had been doing as they hurried toward the newcomers. Seamus Finnigan was among the first, his battered face splitting into an enormous grin, followed closely by Ernie Macmillan and several others who had fought alongside Harry in Dumbledore's Army. Even those who barely knew him crowded forward, their expressions bright with an excitement Harry hadn't seen in what felt like ages.
Neville emerged behind them, looking immensely pleased with himself. "Told you they'd come back, didn't I?"
That earned another round of cheers, and before Harry could properly respond, he found himself surrounded by familiar faces. Hands clapped him on the shoulders, students called out questions faster than he could answer them, and somewhere beside him Ron was being enthusiastically greeted by Seamus while Hermione struggled to make herself heard above the noise. Harry could scarcely believe the reception. He had expected questions, perhaps even anger at his prolonged absence, but the faces turned toward him were filled with such unmistakable relief that he found himself smiling despite everything.
Then Draceana Malfoy stepped out of the passage.

text:
The 2030 Catalyst: How Morocco is Turning a World Cup into a Masterclass in Economic Strategy

When Morocco was announced as a co-host for the FIFA World Cup 2030 alongside Spain and Portugal, the global sports world cheered. But almost immediately, a familiar chorus of critics emerged, asking a seemingly logical question: Why is a developing nation spending billions on shiny football stadiums when that money could go toward schools and hospitals?

It is a valid emotional argument, but it completely misses the bigger picture. Morocco isn't just throwing a month-long party; it is pulling off a massive, highly calculated $20 billion to $23 billion economic transformation. By using the World Cup as a strict, unyielding deadline, the North African kingdom is forcing a decade’s worth of vital national infrastructure into existence. Far from robbing the social safety net, Morocco is building the exact economic super-grid required to fund those very schools and hospitals for generations to come.

Beyond the Pitch: A Smart Breakdown of the Investment

Morocco’s mega-investment plan is strategically divided across the key sectors of its economy, ensuring every dollar spent builds permanent value

The Stadium Edge: Why Casablanca Will Likely Host the Final

At the center of the critic's target is the Grand Stade Hassan II near Casablanca. Budgeted at over $500 million, this 100-hectare architectural marvel draws inspiration from a traditional Moroccan tent. But it isn't just a vanity project—it is a lethal revenue generator.

With an unprecedented 115,000-seat capacity, Casablanca’s mega-stadium is heavily favored by sports diplomats to host the World Cup 2030 Final, beating out Madrid’s legendary Santiago Bernabéu. The math is simple: the Bernabéu caps out at 85,000 seats. Casablanca offers FIFA an extra 30,000 ticket sales per match, alongside 12,000 ultra-premium VIP and luxury corporate boxes. 

Furthermore, giving the final to Casablanca sends a powerful geopolitical message, honoring Africa's soaring football dominance on a purpose-built, state-of-the-art stage.

Silencing the Critics: The Real Macroeconomic Repercussions

The "stadiums vs. schools" argument relies on a false dilemma—the idea that money spent on a sports venue is money stolen from a clinic. In reality, Morocco's financial model is a blueprint for smart emerging-market development.

Instead of draining the central government's general budget (the fund that actually pays for teachers, doctors, schools, and hospitals), Morocco is routing over 100 billion dirhams of project spending through public-private partnerships (PPPs), international infrastructure loans, and state-owned corporate equity. This clever "off-budget" funding structure shields daily social spending from tournament costs.

Furthermore, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) notes that increasing infrastructure spending by just 1% of GDP can boost Morocco’s long-term economic output by around 4% over time. This shift is vital. For decades, Morocco’s GDP has been at the mercy of unpredictable droughts because agriculture employs a third of its workforce. By using the World Cup to turbocharge transport, tourism, tech, and banking, Morocco is intentionally breaking its dependence on the weather.

The immediate payoff is an injection of 100,000 construction and logistics jobs that act as an urgent urban economic cushion. The long-term payoff is a modernized, 5G-enabled, high-speed nation that attracts foreign factories and global corporations. text:
Manack provides a description of how wampum, or sewan, was made: “The Indians divided their beads into two general classes, the ‘wompam,’ derived from ‘wompi’ or ‘white,’ and ‘sukauhock,’ a compound word combining ‘sucki’ or ‘dark colored’ and ‘hock’ or shell. The white wampum was created from the central column of the whelk shell, and the black was composed of the eye of hard-shell clams.”

As currency in New Netherland, clam-based wampum was widely used, with four purple beads or eight white beads equaling one guilder. The 1641 Lion Daalder was equal to two guilders (top right, modern reproduction). The bottom left shows a modern reproduction of a Dutch stiver; twenty-four stivers equaled one guilder, or forty-eight equaled one Lion Daalder. The bottom right is a modern reproduction of a ducaton, worth three guilders and three stivers. It is important to remember that the vast majority of bullion did not circulate within the colony itself, trade goods and pelts were the essential mediums of exchange.

The Dutch West India Company’s regulation of wampum prior to the English takeover in 1664 effectively froze exchange rates. At the same time, the supply of beaver pelts declined, forcing their value in guilders to rise. A single fathom (about 360 beads) equaled roughly 4 guilders and 10 stivers, underscoring the enormous scale of such payments. Even smaller bounties were substantial: 10 fathoms equaled about 45 guilders, and 20 fathoms about 90 guilders.

Richard Manack identifies a case of wampum-based extortion along the Connecticut River in 1622, when 140 fathoms were demanded for the return of Pequot Grand Sachem Tatobem. This amounted to roughly 50,400 beads, nearly 1,000 guilders, or about $100,000 in modern terms,at a time when the average annual income was only about 300 guilders.

The Iroquois League typically required ten fathoms of wampum as compensation for a murdered man and twenty fathoms for a murdered woman. The family of the offender could often pay an additional ten fathoms to avoid execution or the adoption of the killer into the bereaved clan. Dutch authorities adopted these same compensation rates for their own murdered citizens; official proclamations offered identical rewards in exchange for Native perpetrators being turned in. However, few have explicitly connected these Dutch policies to the broader wampum-based restitution systems of neighboring Native societies.

“On Thursday, being the 4th of July (1641), whereas the Indians of the Raritan are daily exhibiting more and more hostility… we have therefore considered it most expedient… to induce the Indians, our allies hereabout, to take up arms… and in order to encourage them the more we have promised them ten fathoms of seawan for each head, and… 20 fathoms… for each head.”

Translation: K. Scott and K. Stryker-Rodda, eds., New York Historical Manuscripts: Dutch, vol. 4, Council Minutes, 1638–1649, trans. A. J. F. van Laer (Baltimore: Genealogical Publishing Co., 1974).

text:
Let’s talk Wampum:

“Their money consists of certain little bones, made of shells or cockles, which are found on the sea-beach; a hole is drilled through the middle of the little bones, and these they string upon thread, or they make of them belts as broad as a hand, or broader, and hang then on their necks, or around their bodies. They have also several holes in their ears, and there they likewise hang some. They value these little bones as highly as Christians do gold, silver and pearls; but they do not like our money, and esteem it no better than iron. I once showed one of their chiefs a rix-dollar; he asked how much it was worth among the Christians; and when I told him, he laughed exceedingly at us, saying we were fools to value a piece of iron so highly; and if he had such money, he would throw it into the river.”
-Johannes Megapolensis, August 22nd, 1644

“That there should be no miserly desire for the costly metals among the natives, few will believe; still it is true, the use of gold and silver or any metallic coin is unknown among them. The currency which they use in their places to which they resort is called wampum, the making and preparing of which is free to all persons. The species are black and white, but the black is worth more by one half than the white. The black wampum is made from conch shells, which are to be taken from the sea, or which are cast ashore from the sea twice a year. They strike off the thin parts of those shells and preserve the pillars or standards, which they grind smooth and even and reduce the same according to their thickness, and drill a hole through every piece and string the same on strings, and afterwards sell the strings of wampum in that manner. This is the only article of moneyed medium among the natives, with which any traffic can be driven; and it is also common with us in purchasing necessaries and carrying on our trade; many thousand strings are exchanged every year for peltries near the seashore where the wampum is only made, and where the peltries are brought for sale. Among the Netherlanders gold and silver begin to increase and are current, but still the amount differs much from that of the Netherlands.”
-Adriaen van der Donck “Description of New Netherland”

text: The amazing thing about Hawaii is that although it's part of the USA, it often feels overlooked by the rest of the country. Hawaii rarely dominates national headlines or elections. In many ways it's America, but not quite. It has security, prosperity, stability, and resources from the American system, without many of the problems that come with the mainland's "cursed geography." The isolation and distance at first feels strange, but once you get used to it, you learn how special the "island life" really is. As they say, "Distance makes the heart grow fonder." Maybe that's part of Hawaii's magic. You're far enough away from the world to appreciate it, but still close enough to enjoy everything it has to offer. A peaceful, secure, beautiful, healthy, loving, and warm island full of many amazing people... It's cool to be in a place that feels so far removed from everything, yet still enjoys the advantages of being connected. I love Hawaii.

text:
The most interesting question about the AI boom may not be whether the technology works.

It may be whether the returns arrive on the same timetable as the bills.

In October 2025, investors bought $27.3 billion of bonds to finance a Meta data center in Louisiana. A year later, those bonds were reported trading around 91 cents on the dollar. That price doesn't tell us the project will fail. It tells us the market's valuation of the debt has changed.

Alphabet's latest quarterly results offer another perspective: $51.4 billion in capital spending and negative free cash flow. A fine payment and inventory also affected cash flow, so this isn't simply a story of construction swallowing cash.

But the underlying tension is worth thinking about. Capital is committed today. The returns must justify it over time.

India is part of this buildout too. Google's announced $15 billion AI hub in Vizag brings that global question closer to home, even if its financing is different.

A useful technology and a good investment are not automatically the same thing.

Conviction can move quickly. Infrastructure pays back on its own clock.

Who carries the cost when those clocks don't agree?

#AI #Investing #Infrastructure

WASHINGTON — US President Donald Trump says the US military has carried out new limited strikes on Iran, targeting an Iranian air defense system.
Iranian state media had reported the sound of two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which is in the crucial waterway for oil shipments.

Trump in an exchange with reporters describes the military action as “minor.”

“They knocked out — they built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five,” Trump tells reporters shortly after arriving in West Palm Beach, Florida.

Trump doesn’t offer further details about the target. But US officials have reported that most of Iran’s air defense systems were destroyed or severely degraded during a June 2025 bombardment by #Israel and in the early stages of the current conflict. US officials have assessed that Iran would try to rebuild them and other military infrastructure over time.

The strikes are the first since Trump’s Republican Party was dealt a stunning repudiation in Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US.

The electoral setback — Republicans lost both chambers of Congress — was stoked in part by voter dissatisfaction with Trump’s execution of the conflict and elevated fuel prices, a byproduct of the war that’s affected nearly every sector of the global economy.

In the days since Republicans’ shellacking at the polls, Trump has vacillated between threatening to “destroy” Iran and suggesting a resolution to the war is near.

text:
@omar_quraishi Thank you for a thoughtful and well argued article. Your distinction between American electoral politics and enduring strategic interests is persuasive. However, I believe your conclusion gives insufficient weight to the distinction between Washington’s relationship with Pakistan and its relationship with those who exercise power within Pakistan.

Pakistan’s strategic importance may endure. American backing for particular rulers is considerably more conditional.

Washington has often found military rulers convenient partners because concentrated authority facilitates specific security objectives. But past services do not guarantee future protection. A ruler’s usefulness can diminish even while the country’s importance remains unchanged.

Egypt offers a relevant comparison. Hosni Mubarak, a former air force commander and longstanding American ally, lost Washington’s backing during the 2011 uprising. Power passed to the military council headed by Field Marshal Hussein Tantawi. Following Mohamed Morsi’s elected presidency, the military removed him in 2013, and Field Marshal Abdel Fattah el Sisi subsequently became president. This does not establish that Washington orchestrated these transitions. It illustrates how an individual ruler can become dispensable while the military institution retains its central position. We might see a similar distinction emerge in Pakistan, with support for particular military leaders weakening while cooperation with the institution continues.

Musharraf’s experience also demonstrates the limits of personal alignment with an American president. His close relationship with President Bush did not prevent congressional pressure and American demands for a return to civilian democratic government when his position became increasingly contentious.

This is where stronger congressional constraints on presidential power matter. The president retains substantial authority over foreign affairs, but a more assertive Congress can weaken the political protection extended to favoured foreign partners through hearings, funding conditions and public scrutiny.

Democrats would not need to reverse policy towards Pakistan to challenge Trump’s relationship with its present power holders. Even opposition driven partly by domestic political rivalry could make that relationship more difficult to sustain.

Nor would a reassessment necessarily mean abandoning Pakistan’s military establishment. Washington could become more receptive to a credible democratic arrangement, or to a different military figure whom it considers better able to protect its interests and maintain stability.

My argument is therefore about the vulnerability of the present leadership, rather than an inevitable American preference for democracy. If internal discontent makes particular rulers a source of instability, Pakistan’s strategic importance could become a reason to favour their replacement rather than preserve them.

The midterms may change relatively little about why Washington needs Pakistan, while changing considerably more about whom Washington is willing to support within it.

Continuity towards Pakistan should not be confused with immunity for its rulers.

text:
Why the US midterms won’t change much for Pakistan 

By Omar Quraishi

The Friday Times 

November 5

The United States midterm elections may have delivered a significant political setback to the Republican Party and President Donald Trump, but their implications for American foreign policy are likely to be considerably less dramatic than some observers might imagine. While the electoral results may reshape the domestic political landscape, alter the balance of power in Congress and complicate the administration’s legislative agenda, they do not necessarily herald a fundamental change in how Washington engages with the rest of the world. This is particularly true in the case of Pakistan, whose growing regional importance and evolving strategic relationships have increasingly become factors that American policymakers cannot afford to overlook.

There is a tendency, especially outside the United States, to interpret American elections as potential turning points in Washington’s relationships with other countries. This is understandable, given the enormous influence the United States continues to exercise over international politics, global financial institutions, security arrangements and diplomatic initiatives. However, the reality is that American foreign policy generally displays a remarkable degree of continuity, regardless of which political party controls Congress or occupies the White House.

Certainly, differences exist between Republican and Democratic administrations. Their approaches to multilateralism, international institutions, trade, immigration and military intervention can vary considerably. Yet beneath these differences lies a broad consensus on protecting American strategic interests, maintaining alliances, preserving military influence and preventing rival powers from challenging Washington’s global position.

This continuity is not accidental. American foreign policy is shaped not merely by elected politicians but also by a vast institutional structure comprising the State Department, the Pentagon, intelligence agencies, congressional committees and an extensive network of strategic and economic interests. These institutions often operate within long-established policy frameworks that survive changes in political leadership.

Consequently, even a substantial shift in congressional control does not automatically translate into a corresponding transformation of America’s international relationships.

There is another important consideration. President Trump will remain in office for approximately two more years. Whatever the domestic political consequences of the midterms, the presidency retains considerable authority over foreign affairs. The White House continues to direct diplomacy, conduct negotiations, manage international crises and exercise significant influence over national security decisions.

Congress can certainly impose constraints through legislation, budgetary allocations, oversight and the approval of certain appointments. Nevertheless, the president remains the central figure in the formulation and execution of American foreign policy. For countries dealing with Washington, including Pakistan, the administration’s priorities will therefore remain critically important.

In Pakistan’s case, the argument for continuity becomes even more compelling when viewed against the changing strategic environment in South Asia and the wider region.

Pakistan today occupies a position of considerable geopolitical importance. Its location at the intersection of South Asia, Central Asia, China, Afghanistan and the Middle East gives it a relevance that extends far beyond its immediate neighbourhood. Its military capabilities, nuclear deterrent, longstanding relationship with China and engagement with major Muslim countries make it an important participant in regional security calculations.

Recent diplomatic developments, including the emergence of the Makkah Alliance and the Badar Alliance, have added another dimension to this evolving strategic landscape.

These arrangements, and the broader diplomatic and security cooperation associated with them, represent an attempt to develop new frameworks for regional engagement, conflict prevention and collective security. Their long-term significance will depend on how effectively participating countries translate political understandings into institutional cooperation and practical outcomes.

For Pakistan, however, their importance lies in the opportunity to play a more consequential role in shaping regional security discussions rather than merely responding to developments initiated elsewhere.

The Middle East and South Asia are undergoing profound geopolitical changes. Traditional alliances are being reassessed, economic relationships are becoming increasingly important, and countries are seeking greater flexibility in their strategic partnerships. The growing emphasis on regional dialogue and security cooperation reflects an understanding that lasting stability cannot depend exclusively on arrangements designed by outside powers.

Pakistan’s participation in these developments potentially strengthens its diplomatic position and provides additional avenues through which it can contribute to regional stability.

Washington will naturally evaluate such initiatives through the prism of American interests. It will examine their implications for regional security, relations with Iran, the Gulf states, China and other influential actors. But precisely because these developments affect important strategic interests, they are unlikely to be ignored simply because the political composition of Congress has changed.

This is an important distinction. Pakistan’s relationship with the United States should not be understood exclusively through the personalities occupying the White House or the electoral fortunes of either major American political party. It is also shaped by structural considerations that extend across administrations.

These include regional security, counterterrorism cooperation, developments in Afghanistan, nuclear stability, economic engagement and the wider strategic competition involving China. While the relative importance attached to these issues may change, the underlying interests do not disappear after an election.

At the same time, Pakistan should avoid assuming that its geopolitical importance automatically guarantees favourable treatment from Washington. Strategic relevance creates opportunities, but those opportunities must be supported by diplomatic consistency, economic credibility and clearly articulated national priorities.

The Makkah and Badar initiatives, for example, will acquire lasting significance only if they demonstrate their ability to facilitate dialogue, reduce tensions and contribute meaningfully to regional stability. Their success cannot be measured simply by the number of participating countries or the declarations issued at diplomatic gatherings.

For Islamabad, the appropriate response to developments in American domestic politics is therefore neither excessive optimism nor unnecessary apprehension. It is sustained diplomatic engagement based on an understanding of how American institutions function and how Pakistan’s own strategic position is evolving.

There is also a broader lesson here. International relationships are increasingly shaped by multiple centres of power. Countries such as Pakistan have opportunities to diversify their diplomatic partnerships without necessarily abandoning longstanding relationships. Engagement with Washington need not come at the expense of cooperation with Beijing, Riyadh, Ankara, Tehran or other regional capitals.

Indeed, maintaining productive relationships across competing geopolitical groupings may become an increasingly important element of Pakistan’s foreign policy.

The American midterms may influence the political atmosphere in Washington, sharpen partisan disagreements and affect the administration’s room for manoeuvre. They could also alter congressional scrutiny of foreign assistance, trade and security cooperation. These are developments Islamabad should monitor carefully.

But it would be a mistake to confuse changes in America’s domestic political balance with an inevitable transformation of its international priorities.

Ultimately, American foreign policy will continue to be determined by calculations of national interest, strategic necessity and global influence. Pakistan’s task is to ensure that its own foreign policy is similarly grounded in long-term national interests rather than short-term political developments abroad.

The coming two years will undoubtedly produce further diplomatic challenges and opportunities. President Trump will remain a decisive actor in American international relations, while Pakistan’s expanding regional engagements will continue to shape its strategic choices.

The real question, therefore, is not whether the American midterms will fundamentally change Washington’s approach towards Pakistan. It is whether Pakistan can translate its growing diplomatic engagement and strategic importance into durable economic, political and security gains.

That, far more than the electoral fortunes of Republicans or Democrats, will determine the future direction of Pakistan’s relationship with the United States.

The writer is a journalist based in Karachi.

text:
🇺🇸⚔️🇮🇷Trump’s Iran War Risks Global Economic Collapse as Qeshm Strikes Intensify and Tehran Warns of Devastating Retaliation

President Donald Trump’s continuing war with Iran is threatening to push an already strained global economy towards a deeper crisis, as fresh strikes near the Strait of Hormuz expose the growing dangers of Washington’s military strategy.

Iranian media reported that two projectiles struck the Suza area of Qeshm Island after witnesses heard an aircraft overhead. The extent of any damage remained unclear. US officials acknowledged carrying out limited strikes against Iranian air defences, describing them as defensive, even as regional diplomacy struggled to prevent renewed fighting.

The confrontation has sharpened criticism of Trump’s insistence that military pressure can force Tehran into submission. University of Tehran professor Mohammad Marandi warned that “the US is digging the hole deeper,” adding that further attacks could prompt Iran to “strike back very hard.”

Washington has meanwhile offered up to $20 million, and possible relocation, for intelligence concerning Iran’s nuclear facilities, equipment, scientists and personnel. The announcement raises an uncomfortable question for a president who previously declared Iran’s nuclear programme obliterated: why is his government now paying millions to locate its remaining capabilities?

Security concerns are also spreading beyond Iran. Israel’s Ynet reported that American diplomatic missions across the Middle East had been warned to heighten vigilance amid fears of attacks targeting US officials and a rapid escalation. Reports of intense military aviation activity near the Iran-Iraq border further illustrated the tense atmosphere, although those claims remained independently unconfirmed.

The economic stakes extend far beyond the battlefield. A prolonged confrontation around Hormuz, a vital artery for international energy shipments, risks disrupting oil and gas supplies, inflating transport costs and driving up food prices. Import-dependent economies, particularly in Africa and Asia, could suffer heavily from decisions taken in Washington.

Qatar continues mediating proposals intended to end the conflict, demonstrating that diplomatic alternatives have not disappeared. Yet Trump’s repeated resort to force threatens to undermine those efforts.

Global economic collapse is not inevitable, but neither is it an empty warning. The longer Washington substitutes airstrikes and coercion for negotiation, the greater the danger that a regional conflict becomes an international economic emergency, with devastating consequences for households.

text:
🇺🇸 🇮🇷 US Puts $20 Million Bounty on Iran’s Nuclear Secrets as Military Pressure Mounts

The United States has publicly offered up to $20 million for tips that could map remaining Iranian nuclear facilities, equipment, and key scientists, signaling that American military and intelligence superiority remains the decisive factor in denying Tehran a bomb.

The State Department’s Rewards for Justice program, amplified by U.S. Central Command, is seeking precise details on sites, centrifuges, related technologies, and personnel in the scientific community, along with possible relocation for informants. Official statements cite Iran’s breaches of IAEA safeguards that have created gaps in knowledge about enrichment activities and component inventories. Iran remains the only non-nuclear-weapon state producing uranium at 60 percent purity, a short technical step from weapons-grade material that experts say could yield several devices if further processed.

This public bounty arrives amid an ongoing confrontation in which U.S. forces have already conducted major strikes on Iranian nuclear infrastructure. President Trump has repeatedly stated that those operations inflicted monumental damage and effectively obliterated key elements of the program, while also noting that Tehran continues to signal interest in a deal. The reward offer makes clear that Washington intends to maintain full visibility into any residual or reconstituted capabilities rather than relying solely on past strikes or diplomatic talks.

For decades, successive Iranian governments have pursued enrichment and related work despite international pressure. The combination of demonstrated American strike capacity and now an open financial incentive for insider information underscores a strategy of sustained military and intelligence dominance. Allies, including Israel, have long viewed a nuclear-armed Iran as an existential threat; the current U.S. posture treats prevention of that outcome as a core national-security priority rather than a matter for multilateral consensus alone.

Rewards for Justice has operated since 1984 to buy actionable intelligence that protects American lives and interests. The $20 million ceiling and relocation option are designed to reach scientists, technicians, and others with direct knowledge who might otherwise remain silent. Whether the tips arrive through official channels, Signal, or Tor-based lines, the message is that U.S. military reach and the ability to act on intelligence remain intact.

In practical terms, the initiative reduces Iran’s room to hide residual enrichment capacity or move equipment and personnel. It also reinforces the broader point that American conventional and intelligence advantages continue to set the terms of the conflict, limiting Tehran’s options even as talks continue. The bounty is less a sign of uncertainty than a tool of ongoing supremacy: the United States can both strike and systematically buy the knowledge needed to strike again if required.

Nov 2026 — AI stack notes from a heavy user in Hong Kong who travels to mainland China a lot.

Top pick right now: Grok Bot, Codex, Kimi, Genspark.

Grok Bot — day-to-day operator layer
Super connector of second brain, multi agent workflow and AI subscription controls. Works from Hong Kong for the daily workflow.

Codex — real code and long agent jobs
Great CP value per intelligence. The path that works from Hong Kong: VPN / nest Codex inside Grok Bot. The bot’s computer runs in US cloud, so that job does not need a local VPN to OpenAI.

Kimi — continuity when you cross the border
Desktop widgets for live monitoring. Best chat sync stability across devices I’ve used across Chinese and Western worlds. Native remote computer. This is the layer I rely on when Western surfaces aren’t available on the mainland.

Supporting layer (after the core is stable)
Genspark Claw / Speakly — Claw is great for initial computer setup even for free tiers; Speakly is useful on phone and computer; Genspark offers phone-call and WhatsApp-controlled AI for quick sharing. Best external AI connector so far from the core 3.

GLM on https://t.co/boVpu2W3nE / https://t.co/uG7NeGxWQg — generous API, frequent free resets, ZCode integrates cleanly; one account can mint multiple API keys.

Claude — Hong Kong and mainland both sit outside Anthropic’s supported regions; access got meaningfully harder. Gets blocked easily.

On Phone wake / call-level alerts
Grok Bot — available, but needs a US phone.
Manus — available, but needs a further purchase.
Genspark — works better with an existing phone, no further buy.

Working rule
High security office work already means VPN to office network is daily routine. Don’t add another tunnel just to keep a model alive. And don’t collapse mainland China and Hong Kong into one access story for AI, treat them differently.

text:
But Voldemort had already dismissed her with a contemptuous turn of his head.
Lucius opened his mouth again, but Voldemort raised a hand, silencing him before he could utter another plea.
"Enough. I have heard quite enough of your excuses."
The room fell silent. Voldemort's gaze passed over the kneeling Malfoys and Bellatrix without the slightest interest in what more they might have to say. Harry could still feel his suspicion, but it had become a trivial irritation beside the far more pressing matter occupying his thoughts. Let them plead, let them invent whatever explanations they wished. He had something considerably more important to attend to.
The cup.
Harry felt the thought strike Voldemort with a force that made his scar throb. For all his rage at Bellatrix, for all his suspicions concerning the Malfoys, those matters were becoming insignificant beside one terrible possibility.
Someone knew.
Someone had discovered a secret Voldemort believed no other living person could possibly possess. Fear surged through Harry again, sharper now that it was no longer buried beneath the confusion of the confrontation. Voldemort was afraid of what the theft might mean, afraid that Gringotts had not been chosen at random.
And with that fear came memories.
The drawing room began to fade. In its place, Harry saw an old, ruined house standing amid tangled vegetation. The Gaunt shack, where Dumbledore had found the ring. Before Harry could properly examine it, the image vanished, replaced by a dark cavern and an underground lake surrounding a small island of stone.
The locket's hiding place.
Then came a black diary, its pages opening briefly before disappearing beneath a flash of gold.
Hufflepuff's cup.
Harry could feel Voldemort's thoughts moving rapidly from one hiding place to another, following the terrible possibility that had taken hold of him. The diary had been destroyed. The ring was no longer where he had concealed it. The locket had been removed from its hiding place, and now the cup had been stolen from Bellatrix's vault.
His Horcruxes.
Someone was hunting them.
The realization filled Voldemort with a horror so profound that Harry almost forgot the pain of his scar. This was the secret upon which the Dark Lord had built his certainty of immortality, the knowledge he had guarded more carefully than anything else. To discover that someone might have uncovered it was almost beyond his comprehension.
And then Harry saw Hogwarts.
The castle rose against a pale sky, its towers unmistakable even through the haze. A fierce certainty accompanied the image. Whatever Voldemort had hidden there, he believed it safe, beyond the reach of anyone who might think to search for it. Harry struggled to follow the memory, searching desperately for a glimpse of the object or its hiding place. But Voldemort's thoughts offered him nothing more than the castle itself.
There was another Horcrux at Hogwarts.
Before Harry could discover anything else, the castle disappeared, replaced by the enormous dark-scaled body of a snake.
Nagini.
Voldemort's thoughts changed immediately. The snake must remain close. She must be protected, kept beyond the reach of anyone who might seek to harm her. Harry recognized the same fierce possessiveness, the same terror of loss that had accompanied the memories of the other objects.
A dreadful realization began to form.
Nagini was another Horcrux.
The discovery had scarcely registered when another surge of agony tore through his skull. Hogwarts vanished, followed by the snake, and the last remnants of Voldemort's thoughts dissolved into darkness.
Harry felt himself falling.
Somewhere far away, beyond the rushing sound filling his ears, a voice was calling his name.
"Harry! Harry, please!"
Draceana.
He struggled toward the sound, desperate to escape the terrible fury that still seemed to cling to his consciousness. For one fleeting moment, he thought he could feel her hands gripping his shoulders again.
Then the vision broke.
******
Harry awoke to a dull ache behind his forehead. His eyelids felt heavy, and for several moments, he could make little sense of the darkness surrounding him. The terrible fury that had overwhelmed his consciousness was gone, leaving him with a throbbing headache and the distant crackling of a fire. He blinked several times, trying to bring his surroundings into focus, until he became aware of something warm wrapped around his hand.
"Potter?"
Harry turned toward the voice, and the first thing he saw clearly was Draceana's face.
For a moment, he could only look at her. After the distorted images of Malfoy Manor, Voldemort's fury, and the terrible sensation of being trapped inside another man's mind, the sight of her sitting beside him brought an almost overwhelming sense of relief. She was real, and so was the warmth of her hand around his. He was back.
Draceana was wrapped in a thick blanket, with a towel draped around her shoulders and over her still-damp platinum-blonde hair. Her face was pale, and the firelight did little to conceal the redness around her eyes. She looked as though she had been crying, or had come dangerously close to it. Yet when she noticed his eyes moving toward her, she straightened immediately, recovering an expression of stern composure that might have been convincing if she hadn't been gripping his hand quite so tightly.
"You're awake," she whispered.
Harry managed a faint smile. "Looks that way."
He attempted to sit up, but the lingering pain in his head made him wince. Draceana immediately moved closer, supporting his back with one arm while keeping hold of his hand with the other.
"Slowly." She helped him settle against the folded blankets behind him before studying his face again. "How's your head? Does it still hurt?"
"A bit," Harry admitted. "Nothing like before, though." He glanced around, noticing the small campfire burning nearby and the tent standing beneath the trees. Beyond the firelight, the riverbank had disappeared into darkness. "How long was I out?"
"Hours," Draceana answered, her voice unusually subdued. "Granger said you needed rest, but you wouldn't wake up. We tried everything we could think of."
Harry looked back at her. She was still holding his hand, her fingers tightening whenever he shifted, and he noticed how closely she watched him, as though expecting him to collapse again at any moment. The sight made his expression soften, although he couldn't quite resist the opportunity.
"Were you worried about me?"
"Worried?" Draceana repeated, looking almost offended. "Why on earth would I be worried about you, Potter?"
Harry raised an eyebrow.
"Of course I wasn't," she continued, lifting her chin.
She held his gaze for another moment, apparently determined to maintain her indignant expression. But Harry noticed her lower lip trembling slightly, and when she glanced down at their joined hands, the last of her composure began to falter.
"...Maybe a little," she admitted.
Harry's teasing smile faded.
Draceana drew an uneven breath, tightening her grip around his fingers. "You really scared me, Harry."
There was something painfully honest about the admission. She didn't look at him as she said it, and Harry could see how much effort it had taken her to force the words out. He remembered the last thing he'd heard before the vision swallowed him: Draceana calling his name, begging him to look at her. He hadn't been able to answer then.
"I'm sorry," he said quietly.
Draceana shook her head, but before she could recover enough to dismiss his apology, Harry brought their joined hands closer and gently brushed his thumb across her knuckles. Her eyes lifted to his, and for a moment neither spoke. Then she moved closer, resting her forehead against his shoulder. Harry slipped an arm around her, drawing the blanket more securely around them as she leaned into him.
They remained that way for a while. Draceana's breathing gradually steadied against his shoulder, and Harry found himself listening to the quiet crackling of the fire. He was grateful for the warmth of her beside him, particularly after the cold terror of the vision.
Then he remembered Lucius and Narcissa.
Harry looked down at Draceana, remembering how often she had asked about her parents since Shell Cottage. He had never been able to give her an answer before, but now he finally had something to tell her.
"Draceana," he said softly. "There's something I need to tell you."
She stirred and lifted her head. "What is it?"
"It's about your parents."
Her expression changed immediately. She straightened, the blanket slipping from one shoulder as her fingers tightened painfully around his hand.
"What about them?"
Harry hesitated, searching for the right words. "When I passed out, I saw Voldemort. I was seeing through his eyes, and he was at your manor." He paused, making sure she was listening. "Your mum and dad were there, Draceana. I saw them."
She stared at him without speaking.
"They're alive," Harry continued gently. "Both of them."
For several seconds, Draceana didn't move. Then her lips parted, and she shook her head faintly, as though she hadn't quite understood what he'd said.
"Don't joke about that, Potter." Her voice was barely above a whisper. "I swear, if you're—"
"I'm not joking." Harry looked directly into her eyes. "I saw them. Your father and your mother. They're alive."
"Are you... are you sure?"
"Yes. I'm sure."
Draceana lowered her gaze. Her fingers remained wrapped around his hand, but the tension in her shoulders slowly gave way. She drew a long, unsteady breath, then another, pressing her free hand against her mouth as though trying to steady herself.
Harry watched her quietly. He wished he could offer her more than this. Her parents were still under Voldemort's control, and there was nothing he could do to help them. He couldn't even promise that they would remain safe. Yet when Draceana finally looked up, her eyes were shining.
"Thank you," she whispered.
Before Harry could respond, she threw her arms around him and buried her face against his chest. The sudden movement caught him by surprise, but he quickly wrapped his arms around her, holding her close as she clutched the back of his shirt.
"Thank you, Harry," she murmured, her voice breaking. "Thank you so much."
A small sob escaped her, followed by another. She pressed her face harder against his chest, trying to smother the sounds, but Harry could feel her trembling in his arms. He rested his cheek against her damp hair and gently rubbed her back, allowing her to cry without drawing attention to it.
It was the first time he had seen her give way quite like this. Draceana had been frightened before, and angry, and even desperate, but she had always tried to recover her pride as quickly as possible. Now, with her face hidden against his chest and her fingers clutching his shirt, she seemed to have forgotten about keeping up appearances altogether.
Harry held her a little tighter.
He hadn't forgotten what her parents had done, nor the terrible things that had happened inside their home. But he knew how much Draceana loved them. Watching her finally release the fear she had carried for weeks, he was glad that even this small piece of news had brought her some comfort.
Some time passed before footsteps sounded beyond the firelight.
"Harry?"
Hermione emerged from between the trees with an armful of fallen branches, Ron following close behind with several more tucked beneath his arm. She stopped when she noticed Harry sitting upright, her expression brightening immediately.
"Harry, you're awake!"
Harry looked up, one arm still around Draceana's shoulders. "Hi, Hermione, Ron."
"Blimey, mate!" Ron exclaimed, dropping his firewood beside the campfire. "You gave us a fright. We thought you were going to be out for the night."
"Sorry," Harry replied with a faint smile. "Didn't exactly plan it."
Hermione hurried closer, looking as though she wanted to examine him from head to toe, but stopped when she noticed Draceana curled against his chest. Her face was still hidden from view, and Harry made no attempt to move her.
"Are you feeling better?" Hermione asked more quietly.
"Yeah. Head still hurts a bit, but I'm all right."
Hermione studied him for another moment before nodding, apparently satisfied that he wasn't about to collapse again.
Ron, meanwhile, had finally noticed Draceana. His eyebrows rose, and he gave Harry a small, approving thumbs-up.
Harry frowned at him. You've got the wrong idea, Ron.
Hermione caught the gesture and promptly nudged Ron in the ribs. He looked at her indignantly, but she merely tilted her head toward the other side of the campfire. After exchanging a brief glance, the two quietly gathered their firewood and moved away, leaving Harry and Draceana undisturbed.
Harry watched them go before lowering his gaze to the girl in his arms. She had grown quieter, although her fingers remained curled tightly around his shirt. He gently brushed a loose strand of platinum-blonde hair away from her face and settled back against the blankets, letting her remain where she was.
There were other things he needed to tell them. But they could wait a little longer. For now, Harry was content to hold Draceana while the fire crackled softly beside them.
******
The four of them sat around the campfire, finally enjoying a little peace after the events of the afternoon. Ron had settled beside Hermione, a blanket draped across their shoulders and their fingers loosely intertwined as they watched the flames consume the branches they had gathered. Opposite them, Harry sat with Draceana resting her head against his shoulder, his arm comfortably wrapped around her beneath their own shared blanket. The pain in his scar had subsided to a faint ache, and Draceana, having recovered somewhat from the overwhelming relief of hearing that her parents were alive, seemed content to remain close to him.
For a while, nobody spoke. The fire crackled softly between them, sending occasional sparks into the night air, while the river continued flowing somewhere beyond the trees. Their clothes were still slightly damp despite Hermione's best efforts, and the exhaustion of the day had begun to settle heavily upon them. Yet there was something pleasant about sitting together like this, with no immediate danger to escape and nothing demanding their attention. For the first time since Gringotts, they could simply enjoy the warmth of the fire and one another's company.
Their quiet respite was eventually interrupted by a small sneeze.
Harry glanced down at Draceana, who had lifted a hand to her nose and was looking thoroughly displeased with herself. "You all right?" he asked, pulling the blanket a little more securely around her shoulders.
"Yes, I'm fine, Potter," she muttered, though another shiver ran through her as she adjusted herself against him. She glanced down at her damp clothes, then at the muddy ground surrounding their little campsite, and her expression soured. "Honestly, this is ridiculous. I'm the heiress to the Malfoy family, and here I am, sitting in the middle of nowhere, soaking wet, covered in dirt, and sleeping in a tent. I certainly don't deserve this sort of treatment."
Ron looked up from the fire, an amused grin spreading across his face. "Blimey, Malfoy. You're back to complaining already? You were having a good cry on Harry's shoulder not long ago."
Draceana immediately straightened. "I was not crying, Weasley!"
"Could've fooled me."
"A Malfoy does not cry," she declared, lifting her chin with as much dignity as she could muster while wrapped in a blanket. "I suggest you get your eyes checked."
"Right. Whatever you say, Princess."
Draceana shot him a murderous look, but Ron merely grinned and reached for another branch to feed the fire. Harry, meanwhile, had turned his face away in an unsuccessful attempt to conceal his amusement.
"Oh, don't you start, Potter," she warned.
"I haven't said anything."
"You were about to."
Harry raised his hands in surrender, though the smile on his face remained. Hermione shook her head at the exchange before shifting closer to Ron beneath their blanket, evidently finding the whole thing rather entertaining.
Draceana sighed and settled back against Harry's shoulder, deciding that neither boy was worth arguing with any further. She watched the flames for a moment before glancing toward the three of them. "Seriously, though. Is this what an adventure with you lot is always like?"
Harry, Ron, and Hermione exchanged a glance. For a moment, none of them answered, until Ron let out a chuckle.
"More or less," Harry admitted. "Although I don't remember getting quite this wet every time."
"Speak for yourself," Ron replied. "I seem to remember spending a fair bit of our second year soaking wet."
"That was hardly the worst thing that happened to us that year," Hermione pointed out.
"That was hardly the worst thing that happened to us that year," Hermione pointed out.
"No, I suppose being chased by giant spiders was worse," Ron muttered, his expression darkening at the memory.
Draceana stared at him. "Giant spiders?"
"Don't ask," Ron said immediately.
Harry grinned. "He wasn't particularly fond of them."
"Not particularly fond?" Ron turned toward him indignantly. "They were the size of horses, Harry!"
"And you followed me anyway."
"Well, someone had to make sure you didn't get yourself killed!"
Hermione gave a quiet laugh. "That does rather sum up most of our time at Hogwarts, doesn't it?"
Draceana looked between them in disbelief. "Unbelievable. To think you three have been getting into this sort of trouble year after year. And here I thought you were simply incapable of following school rules."
"Oh, that too," Harry said.
"Mostly Harry, though," Ron added, looking pleased with himself. "He's the real troublemaker."
Harry turned toward him. "Mind repeating that, mate?"
"Ron's not entirely wrong," Hermione remarked before he could answer. "We do seem to spend an awful lot of time following you around, Harry. Usually trying to stop you from getting into even more trouble."
"Thanks, Hermione. Nice to know I've got such loyal friends."
"You're welcome," she replied with an innocent smile.
Draceana gave a satisfied little hum. "Well, you needn't tell me. Even from the other side of whatever you guys got going on, I knew Potter had an extraordinary talent for getting himself into trouble."
Harry glanced down at her. "Funny. I seem to remember you being responsible for quite a lot of it."
"Me?" Draceana pressed a hand against her chest, looking genuinely offended. "Don't be ridiculous, Potter. I was merely extending my friendship to you when we first met. You're the one who rejected it."
"That was a very interesting way of extending friendship."
"Well, nobody had ever refused me before!" she retorted, as though that explained everything.
Ron gave a disbelieving laugh. "Hang on. Is that why you spent the next six years making our lives miserable? Because Harry wouldn't shake your hand?"
Draceana's cheeks coloured slightly. "Oh, shut up, Weasley! There were plenty of other reasons."
"Such as?"
"Your existence, for one."
"Charming."
Harry chuckled and gave her shoulder a gentle squeeze. "You know, you could've just been nice to Ron and Hermione. We might have got along a lot sooner."
"And lower myself to begging for your friendship?" Draceana scoffed. "Absolutely not, Potter. I have my pride."
"Yes, we've noticed," Hermione remarked dryly.
Draceana turned sharply toward her. "What was that, Granger?"
"Nothing," Hermione replied, hiding a smile behind her cup.
Ron laughed, and Harry soon joined him. Draceana looked thoroughly affronted at having all three of them against her, but the effect was somewhat undermined by the fact that she remained tucked comfortably beneath Harry's arm. She muttered something about the dreadful company she was forced to endure, although she made no attempt to leave.
Their conversation continued for a while, drifting between Ron's complaints about their adventures and Hermione's occasional corrections whenever his recollections became particularly exaggerated. Harry contributed just enough to make matters worse, usually at Ron's expense, while Draceana listened with an increasingly bemused expression. She remembered some of the incidents they mentioned, of course. It was difficult to forget the constant rumours surrounding Potter and his friends at Hogwarts. But hearing them speak about those events now, laughing over experiences that had once been genuinely dangerous, was rather different from hearing the stories whispered around the Slytherin common room.
Draceana glanced at Harry, who was still grinning at something Ron had said.
She thought back to their escape from Gringotts. Impersonating her own aunt had been humiliating enough, and she certainly had no desire to repeat the experience of nearly being buried alive beneath an avalanche of multiplying treasure. Then there had been the dragon, the frantic escape through the underground passages, and that dreadful fall into the river.
It had been absolutely terrifying.
And yet, now that she was sitting beside a warm fire with all four of them safely accounted for, she had to admit that parts of it had been rather exciting.
Merlin, what's wrong with me? she wondered, suppressing a small smile. I'm beginning to sound like Potter.
Luna had once suggested that she might be jealous of Harry and his friends. At the time, Draceana had dismissed the idea as ridiculous. What could she possibly have to envy? She had her own friends, her family's wealth and influence, and a place among the most respectable pure-blood families in Britain.
Yet she couldn't quite dismiss Luna's words now.
Her thoughts wandered to Pansy, Crabbe, and Goyle. They had been her companions for most of her life, Pansy since childhood, while Crabbe and Goyle came from families long associated with the Malfoys. They had shared plenty of laughter and mischief over the years, but Draceana had always kept them at a certain distance. Being a Malfoy meant never quite knowing whether someone genuinely enjoyed her company or merely saw another opportunity to curry favour with her family. She had grown accustomed to their agreement, their willingness to follow her lead, and had seldom allowed herself to question what lay behind it.
Then, in sixth year, she had pushed them away altogether. Voldemort's task had left her unwilling to confide in anyone, and now she hadn't heard from any of them in months. She wondered how they were doing, whether they were still at Hogwarts, and what they might think if they discovered she was presently sitting in Harry Potter's arms. Pansy, in particular, would undoubtedly have plenty to say about that.
Draceana sighed quietly, her gaze settling on the flames. Perhaps, when all of this was over, she ought to seek them out again. She wasn't entirely certain what sort of reception awaited her, but she found herself missing their company nonetheless.
A burst of laughter from Ron drew her attention back to the others. Harry was shaking his head at something his friend had said, while Hermione wore an expression of amused disbelief.
Draceana watched them for a moment, then found herself smiling faintly.
Perhaps Luna hadn't been entirely wrong, after all.
"You know," Harry said, glancing across the fire at Ron and Hermione, "I almost forgot what it was like, the three of us just sitting around talking rubbish. Feels a bit like the old common room, doesn't it?"
Ron glanced across the fire. "What d'you mean?"
"Just sitting around, talking rubbish about things that happened at school." Harry smiled faintly, watching the flames. "Feels like we're back in the Gryffindor common room."
Ron leaned back against the log behind him, considering that for a moment. "Too long, mate. Far too long."
Hermione smiled at the two of them. "I do miss those evenings. Although I seem to remember spending most of them trying to get you two to finish your homework."
"And I seem to remember you never letting us forget it," Ron replied.
"Well, somebody had to make sure you passed your exams."
"See, Harry? Even when we're not at Hogwarts, she's still telling us off."
Harry laughed, earning an exasperated smile from Hermione. It was a familiar exchange, the sort they had shared countless times before, and for a fleeting moment, he could almost picture the old common room again. Ron sprawled across an armchair, Hermione sitting nearby with a book balanced on her knees, and himself trying to finish an essay he should have started several days earlier.
"Funny," Harry murmured. "I never thought I'd miss being nagged about homework."
"There's still time," Hermione replied. "I'm sure I could find you something to study."
"No, thanks. I've changed my mind."

I'm very willing to eat crow on this, but I have a hard time envisioning #Nebraska parting ways with Matt Rhule. 

AD Troy Dannen made a huge mistake last cycle. Instead of daring Rhule to walk and entertain the Penn State job, he caved and offered an extension that has likely handicapped the #Huskers from making a move. 

Never say never, but the math doesn't exactly math for me. Matt Rhule has a $63 million buyout if he's fired this season. I can't see Nebraska ponying up that much money and still having enough in the tank to find a suitable replacement AND fund next year's roster. 

The logical outcome is that Rhule moves on from Holgorsen (sooner rather than later), he sells Dannen on next year's recruiting class (which includes top-ranked QB Trae Taylor) and points to the Aurich hire as a success story. 

Nebraska isn't that far away from being competent. But Rhule's flaws and Dannen's missteps have likely hamstrung this program for the foreseeable future. #Cornhuskers #collegefootball
